CHAPTER-VIII 
 
THE SCHEDULED TRIBES AND OTHER TRADITIONAL FOREST DWELLERS 
(RECOGNITION OF FOREST RIGHTS) ACT, 2006 
`The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of 
Forest Rights) Act, 2006 was enacted to recognize and vest the forest rights and 
occupation in forest land in Forest Dwelling Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional 
Forest Dwellers who have been residing in such forests for generations. Act also 
provides a statutory framework for recording the forest rights so vested and the 
nature of evidence required for such recognition and vesting in respect of forest 
land. The Act also empowers the forest rights holders, Gram Sabha and village 
level institutions to protect the wildlife, forest and biodiversity. 
 
Status of Implementation of the Act  
 
8.2 The implementation of the Act has been carried out since its inception as 
an ongoing process by various State Governments / UT Administrations. Progress 
in implementation of FRA in different States/UTs is furnished by the States/UTs on 
a monthly basis indicating the claims received, titles distributed and the extent of 
forest land for which titles have been distributed. Reports received from the 
States/UTs are compiled and put in public domain. As per the latest information 
reported by States and collated under MPR- FRA is being implemented in States -
20 states 1 UT covering 386 districts. 
 
8.3 On being asked about the details of latest status of implementation of the 
Act with regard to different States/UTs and the number of habitat rights given to 
tribal communities in different States/UTs, the Committee was informed as under. 
 
“FRA is being implemented in States -20 states 1 UT covering 386 
districts.As per the information received from States/ UTs upto 31.01.2025,a 
total of 51,03,764 claims (49,02,427 individual and 2,01,337 community) 
have been filed and 24,98,185 titles (23,80,502 individual and 1,17,683 
community) have been distributed to the extent of 1,91,91,086.66 acres 
(50,89,284.80 acres for individual and 1,41,01,801.87 acres for community) 
of forest land. For recognition of habitat rights for PVTGs, State 
Governments have started the process of vesting rights under Section 3 (1) 

47 
 
(e) of FRA. So far, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh have initiated 
and vested Habitat Rights for 10 PVTGs in 14 districts.”  
 
8.4 On being enquired about effectiveness of the Act in empowering and 
strengthening Tribals including PVTGs, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs inter-alia 
submitted vide their written reply that:- 
“Recently the Government has approved 'Dharti Aaba Janajatiya Gram 
Utkarsh Abhiyan' (DA-JGUA) with the aim of improving the socio-economic 
condition of tribal communities by adopting saturation coverage for tribal 
families in tribal majority villages and Aspirational Districts covering about 
63000 villages. Under DA-JGUA, MoTA is taking various initiatives like the 
Development of State and National FRA Portal and Digitisation of record 
and claim process, Mapping of Potential Forest Rights, Setting up of FRA 
Cells in States, and Support to States for CFR Management. DA-JGUA 
adopts a holistic approach aimed at providing sustainable livelihood to 
Forest-dwelling tribal families who have been vested with Individual and 
Community Forest Rights. Under DA-JGUA, there is a multi-sectoral 
livelihood support component for FRA patta holders in convergence with 
Ministry of Agriculture and Farmer’s Welfare, Department of Fisheries, 
Department of Animal Husbandry. Further, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs 
(MoTA) and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj (MoPR) have collaborated to 
conduct a special capacity-building campaign for the effective 
implementation of FRA and strengthening PESA Gram Sabha under 'Dharti 
Aaba Janajatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan”. 
 
8.5  On being asked about the complaints received in implementing the 
Scheme along with the actions taken, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs submitted vide 
written reply that: 
“the Ministry receive the complaints / grievances through online Centralized 
Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) portal 
wherein a complainant can lodge grievance. Since, January 2020 to 14 
February, 2025, 629 grievances were received by States/UTs out of which 
120 have been disposed of.” 
 
 8.6    With regard to the role of the Ministry of Tribal Affairs in the 
implementation of Forest Rights Act, the Secretary, Ministry of Tribal Affairs, 
deposed before the Committee during oral evidence that : 
 
“we have done three interventions off late.  The first major intervention is to 
try and digitize the process.  Once a person has given a petition, it should be 
visible to all.  Where it is lying and for how many days?  What is the 
disposal?  So, that process is on.  I am happy to say that three States have 
finished the process.  We are giving the money and the technology to help 

48 
 
them do it.  We have also helped the States to have a GIS digitization of 
potential area.  What is happening is this.  Normally there is a conflict 
between the Forest Department and the Tribal Welfare Department.  The 
Forest Department will say, no they do not deserve any patta out of this 
area, etc.  So, we said that we will create FRA atlases.  We have paid 
money and hired technical expertise and NGOs.  So, all the forest area near 
these villages is being mapped. In fact, that process is mostly over and many 
States have published the atlas also. So, that becomes the potential FRA 
area eligible for tribal community. So, at least, the Forest Department in this 
area will not harass. We are formally getting these digital FRA atlases 
published by a State Government. Fortunately, we have a good cooperation. 
In another three months’ time, we will finish the entire FRA in 17 States.”  
 
8.7 The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition 
of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 was enacted to recognize and vest the forest rights 
and occupation in forest land on forest dwelling schedules tribes and other 
traditional forest dwellers. The Committee find that out of the 51,03,764 claims 
filed by Tribals,  24,98,185 titles have been distributed by 31 January, 2025. The 
Committee also find from January, 2020 to February, 2025, out of total number 
of 629 grievances related to FRA received by the States/UTs, only 120 have been 
disposed off.  The Committee strongly feel that there is an urgent need to set up 
an effective grievance redressal mechanism so that the claims filed by Tribals 
are settled within a time frame as State/UT Governments are taking time in 
resolving grievances filed by Tribals.  The Committee also feel that vesting of 
habitat rights to PVTGs is also getting delayed as only three States/UT viz. 
Odisha, Madhya Pradesh and Chattisgarh have initiated the process till date.  
The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry of Tribal Affairs are 
required to take suitable measures and direct all the State Governments/UT 
Administrations to vigorously implement the various provisions of the Act.    
 
8.8 The Committee find that the Ministry of Tribal Affairs  has recently 
launched 'Dharti Aaba Janajatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan' (DA-JGUA). Under the 
Abhiyan, various steps are being taken as regards to implementation of FRA Act 
such as Development of State and National FRA Portal,  digitization of record 
and claim process, mapping of Potential Forest Rights, setting up of FRA Cells 
in States, and support to States for CFR Management. The Committee also find 
that under DA-JGUA, there is a multi-sectoral livelihood support component for 

49 
 
FRA patta holders in convergence with Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ 
Welfare, Department of Fisheries and Department of Animal Husbandry. Further, 
the Ministry of Tribal Affairs and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj have 
collaborated to conduct a special capacity-building campaign for the effective 
implementation of FRA provisions.  The Committee appreciate the efforts made 
by the Ministry and expect that various initiatives taken under DA-JUGA should 
be implemented in a time bound manner so that livelihood support with the 
coordination of various Ministries/Departments are provided to FRA patta 
holders.

Overseas Scholarship Scheme and 750 to 1000 slots under 
National Fellowship & Scholarship Scheme.  The Committee 
appreciate the efforts being made by the Ministry of Tribal 
Affairs for getting additional provision of ₹220 crore and ₹ 
9.25 crore for 2025-26 under both the Schemes and also 
appreciate for considering the requests for Tribal students to 
enhance the number of slots under both the Schemes.  The 
Committee would like the Ministry of Tribal Affairs to also 
consider the request of Tribal students to increase the 
sanctioned amount and incorporate in the proposal to EFC as 
the amount has not been increased for many years.  The 
Committee recommend that the sanctioned amount should 
have inbuilt mechanism to absorb the inflation and also 
desire that the Ministry should pursue with EFC in getting 
proposed additional provision for both the Schemes for 2025-
26 and also ensure that the slots are enhanced for next 
Finance Commission cycle. The Committee would like to be 
apprised on the status of proposal made by the Ministry of 

66 
 
Tribal Affairs to EFC. 
13. 8.7 The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers 
(Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 was enacted to 
recognize and vest the forest rights and occupation in forest 
land on forest dwelling schedules tribes and other traditional 
forest dwellers. The Committee find that out of the 51,03,764 
claims filed by Tribals,  24,98,185 titles have been distributed 
by 31 January, 2025. The Committee also find from January, 
2020 to February, 2025, out of total number of 629 grievances 
related to FRS received by the States/UTs, only 120 have been 
disposed off.  The Committee strongly feel that there is an 
urgent need to set up an effective grievance redressal 
mechanism so that the claims filed by Tribals are settled 
within a time frame as State/UT Governments are taking time 
in resolving grievances filed by Tribals.  The Committee also 
feel that vesting of habitual rights to PVTGs is also getting 
delayed as only three States/UT viz. Odisha, Madhya Pradesh 
and Chattisgarh have initiated the process till date.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry of Tribal 
Affairs are required to take suitable measures and direct all 
the State Governments/UT Administrations to vigorously 
implement the various provisions of the Act.    
14. 8.8 The Committee find that the Ministry of Tribal Affairs  has 
recently launched 'Dharti Aaba Janajatiya Gram Utkarsh 
Abhiyan' (DA-JGUA). Under the Abhiyan various steps are 
being taken as regards to implementation of FRA Act such as 
Development of State and National FRA Portal,  digitization of 
record and claim process, mapping of Potential Forest Rights, 
setting up of FRA Cells in States, and support to States for 
CFR Management. The Committee also find that under DA-
JGUA, there is a multi-sectoral livelihood support component 
for FRA patta holders in convergence with Ministry of 

67 
 
Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, Department of Fisheries, 
Department of Animal Husbandry. Further, the Ministry of 
Tribal Affairs and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj have 
collaborated to conduct a special capacity-building campaign 
for the effective implementation of FRA provisions.  The 
Committee appreciate the efforts made by the Ministry and 
expect that various initiatives taken under DA-JUGA should 
be implemented in a time bound manner so that livelihood 
support with the coordination of various 
Ministries/Departments are provided to FRA patta holders.

REPORT 
 
CHAPTER – I 
 
INTRODUCTORY 
 
 
 The mandate of the Ministry of Minority Affairs includes formulation of overall 
policy and planning, coordination, evaluation and review of the regulatory and 
development programmes for the benefit of the minority communities namely Jains, 
Parsis, Buddhists, Sikhs, Christians and Muslims.  
1.2 The vision of the Ministry is to create an enabling environment for strengthening 
the multi-facial, multi-cultural, multi-lingual and multi-religious character of the nation. 
The mission of the Ministry is to improve the socio-economic condition of the Minority 
communities through an affirmative action and inclusive development so that every 
citizen has equal opportunity and to participate accordingly in building a dynamic 
nation, to facilitate equitable share for Minority communities in education, employment, 
economic activities and to ensure their upliftment.  
1.3 T he following Schemes are being implemented by the Ministry for the welfare 
of Minority Communities: 
 
 
 
I. Pradhan Mantri Jan Vikas Karyakram (PMJVK), a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme of the Ministry provides for development of infrastructure projects in 
Education, Health, Skill Development Sectors and Women-centric projects, for 
improving the socio-economic conditions of people in the identified areas. 
 
II. The Ministry has designed Pradhan Mantri Virasat Ka Samvardhan (PM 
VIKAS), an umbrella scheme by converging five of the existing schemes of the 
Ministry namely –Seekho Aur Kamao, Upgrading the Skills and Training in 
Traditional Arts / Crafts for Development (USTTAD), Hamari Dharohar, Nai 
Roshni and Nai Manzil.  
 
III. The Ministry of Minority Affairs implements three scholarship schemes namely 
Pre-Matric, Post-Matric and Merit-cum-Means based Scholarship Schemes for 
the educational empowerment of notified minority communities. The schemes 
intend to lower the financial burden of financially weaker sections of religious 
minority communities. As part of an overall exercise to harmonize all the 
scholarship schemes of various Ministries/ Departments, the schemes will be 
brought under the ambit of an umbrella scheme. 
  

2 
 
IV. Jiyo Parsi is a Central Sector Scheme concerning the decline of Parsi 
population in India. The scheme has three components, Medical Assistance, 
Advocacy and Health of Community. Since inception, the scheme has enabled 
birth of more than 400 Parsi children till 31.03.2024. 
 
V. The National Minorities Development & Finance Corporation (NMDFC) was 
incorporated on 30.09.1994 as a ‘Not for Profit’ company under Section 25 of the 
Companies Act, 1956 (now Section 8 of Companies Act, 2013). NMDFC provides 
concessional credit viz., Term Loan, Education Loan, Micro Finance & Virasat 
implemented through the State Channelizing Agencies (SCAs) for self-
employment and income generating activities for the socio-economic 
development of the ‘backward sections’ amongst the notified Minorities. 
 
1.4 The Ministry of Minority Affairs had proposed for the Budgetary Allocation of 
₹4381.28 crore for the year 2025-26 for different Schemes. The Ministry of Finance has, 
however, allocated ₹3350.00 crore. The Scheme-wise proposal made by the Ministry

“(i) With the approval of competent authority, 02 schemes namely (a) Free 
Coaching & Allied Scheme, and (b) Nai Udaan, were discontinued from beginning 
of FY 2022-23. Under the Free Coaching and Allied Schemes (Naya Savera) 
wherein coaching was provided to minority youth was discontinued as the New 
Education Policy 2020, does not support coaching programs. Under the Nai 
Udaan scheme financial support was provided to candidates who qualify in the 
preliminary examinations conducted by Union Public Service Commission 
(UPSC), Staff Selection Commission (SSC), State Public Service Commissions 
(SPSCs). As no other Ministry / Department was providing such support to their 
beneficiaries, thus, in order to attain uniformity, the Ministry, decided to 
discontinue the Scheme w.e.f. 2022-23. 
 
(ii) From year 2022-23 onwards, the Pre-Matric Scholarship Scheme is being 
harmonized with the Schemes of other line ministries, Ministry of Social Justice & 
Empowerment, Ministry of Tribal Affairs, etc. Accordingly, the coverage under the 
Pre-Matric Scheme has been restricted to class IX-X, whereas Schemes like 
Padho Pardesh and Maulana Azad National Fellowship have been discontinued 
since 2022-23 due to the fact that there was an overlap of these two schemes 
with the schemes of other Ministries/ Departments.

comprising 2 sub-components namely (i) SPQEM, and (ii) IDMI, was under 
implementation of Department of School Education & Literacy, Ministry of 
Education from 1993-94 to 2020-21. Thereafter, the scheme was transferred to 
the Ministry of Minority Affairs in 2021-22. As the Scheme was approved upto FY 
2021-22, thus, the Ministry of Minority Affairs implemented the scheme upto 2021-
22 only.”

2.5 As regards to policy changes likely to be introduced in 2025-26 for the effective 
implementation of the Schemes and Programmes of the Ministry so that the welfare of 
the notified Minority communities is not compromised, the Committee were informed 
vide written reply that: 
(i) “As per the felt needs on the basis of experience gained during 
implementation and execution of PMJVK and also based on the 
recommendations given by different independent Evaluations Studies during the 
years 2008-09 to 2022, from time to time necessary modifications have been 
carried out in the scheme’ guidelines.  The latest amendments in the PMJVK’ 
Guidelines were carried out in April 2022 inter-alia making it implementable 
across the country irrespective of the declared Minority Concentration Areas 
along with some more changes.  In future also the scheme would be subject to 
modifications as per the requirements. 
(ii) In respect of Scholarship Schemes, as of now, Ministry is making efforts to 
get the schemes approved for implementation at the earliest. 
 (iii) The Ministry has designed and constructed the PM VIKAS scheme 
 considering the specific requirements of the notified minority communities. The 
 scheme aims at providing comprehensive skill development, traditional training, 
 leadership and entrepreneurship promotion and education support to the notified 
 minority communities.”  
 
 
 

8 
 
2.6. The Committee note that the actual expenditure of the Ministry of 
Minority Affairs has gone down considerably during previous years. The 
Ministry could spend only ₹837.68 crore and ₹1,032.65 crore out of 
₹2,612.66 (RE) crore and ₹2,608.93 (RE) crore during the year 2022-23 and 
2023-24 respectively. The situation did not improve in 2024-25 as the 
Ministry were able to spend only ₹919.10 crore out of budgetary allocation 
of ₹3,183.24 crore (BE) by 31 December, 2024. The Committee have been 
apprised that the Ministry have not been able to spend the budgetary 
allocation as several Schemes such as ‘Free Coaching and Allied Scheme’, 
‘Nai Udaan’, ‘Scheme of Providing Education in Madrasas/ Minorities 
(SPEMM)’, etc, have been discontinued and PM-VIKAS launched in 2023-24 
did not initiate. Further, the amount allocated during 2022-23 to 2024-25 
under various  Scholarship Schemes of the Ministry could not be spent 
because these Schemes are under consideration for approval since 2022-
23 as they are being harmonised with the Schemes of other line Ministries, 
viz. Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment and Ministry of Tribal 
Affairs. The Committee strongly believe that the Ministry of Minority Affairs 
are making all efforts to achieve the mission of the Ministry by streamlining 
and strengthening the  prevailing System so that the deserving Minorities 
can avail the benefits of the Schemes and  the funds are not misused. The 
Committee feel that the steps taken by the Ministry were necessary in order 
to harmonize the system with the welfare Schemes of Ministry of Social 
Justice & Empowerment and Ministry of Tribal Affairs and hope that these 
steps will improve the implementation of the Schemes and enhance the  
socio-economic condition of six notified minority communities in the 
country. Since the Ministry of Minority Affairs are in process of 
streamlining/strengthening the prevailing System,  the Committee expect 
that  the necessary approvals will be obtained by the Ministry at the earliest 
so that the allocated Budget of ₹3,350.00 crore for 2025-26 is fruitfully 
utilised. The Committee, therefore, recommend the Ministry of Minority 

9 
 
Affairs to vigorously pursue with the concerned Ministries/ Departments for 
the pending approvals and keep the administrative machinery of the 
Ministry ready for immediate implementation of the Schemes as soon as 
they are approved.

National Fellowship for Minority students came down drastically between 2022-23  
to 2025-26, the representative of the Ministry during the deliberation informed the 
committee as under:  
 
“Under the scholarship components, we have primarily three scholarships – Pre-Matric, 
Post-Matric, and Merit-cum Means scholarship schemes.  These schemes have been 
since 2007-08. 
Regarding these scholarship schemes, approval of the schemes beyond 2021-22 is 
under  consideration. Salient features regarding the scheme, is eligibility criteria. We 
have 50 per cent qualifying marks. I would like to tell you that our scholarship schemes 
are being harmonised with OBC scholarships of Ministry of Social Justice and 
Empowerment regarding rate, annual parental income, funding pattern, and earmarking 
for girls. Sir, 30 per cent of scholarships are earmarked for girls. We have introduced a 
new payment system (Aadhar Payment Bridge System) which was done for 2022-23 
renewal scholarship. 
As far as budgetary allocation is concerned, everything was smooth till 2021-22, 
and, then, after that, we are awaiting pending approval from the Cabinet. We have spent 
some money on the committed liability part. The reason behind the same is this. There 
were media reports in 2020, and the matter was referred to CBI, and then, we had asked 
the States to investigate the cases. Five States have taken active action under these 
cases. If you see here, in Assam, 15 FIRs have been registered and 43 persons have 
been arrested. Cases are ongoing and we are monitoring it on regular basis.” 
 
3.5 As regards to the need to revise the Scheme and the reasons due to 
which extraordinary time being consumed in approval of the Scheme, the Ministry in 
written submission stated that: 
  
“Like Ministry of Minority Affairs, there are other Ministries/ Departments who are 
implementing similar Scholarship Schemes. While drafting the proposal for approval 
of the Scholarship Schemes for the period beyond 2022-23, it was felt to harmonize 
the parameters of the Schemes with similar schemes of other Ministries/ 
Departments so as to main stream the Scheme. This was attempted for ease of 
choosing the Scholarship Scheme by an applicant among all the Central 
Scholarship Schemes. 
  

12 
 
Meanwhile, irregularities were highlighted during the third party evaluation studies. 
To plug out such fraudulent elements from the system, Ministry asked the States to 
take corrective measures including registering FIRs and conduct thorough enquiry.

with conclusive corrective measures taken by the States will make it easier to get 
the scheme approved. In the meanwhile, Ministry also conducted Aadhaar based 
bio-metric authentication drive for all the applicants for the year 2022-23. This entire

CHAPTER-V 
PRADHAN MANTRI JAN VIKAS KARYAKRAM (PMJVK) 
 
  The Pradhan Mantri Jan Vikas Karyakram (PMJVK), erstwhile Multi Sectoral 
Development Programme (MsDP) initiated in the year 2008-09, is a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme(CSS) being implemented from financial year 2017-18 with the objective to 
develop community infrastructure and basic amenities in the identified areas for 
improving the quality of life of the people in these areas. The Minority Concentrated 
Areas (MCAs) were identified on the basis of concentration of minority population and 
backwardness in terms of identified indicators. The areas covered under PMJVK were 
increased from 90 Districts originally, to 308 Districts in 33 States/ UTs w.e.f. May, 2018. 
The scheme has been revised with the approval of the Cabinet in the year 2022 for 
continuation over the 15th Finance Commission Cycle i.e. upto 2025-26. The Scheme is 
now implementable in all Districts across the Country including all the Aspirational 
Districts subject to fulfilling of crieteria that the place of infra-development under the 
scheme should have more than 25% Minority Population within the catchment area of 15 
kms.  
  
5.2 As per procedure the proposals under PMJVK are recommended by the State 
Level Committee (SLC) headed by the Chief Secretary of the respective States/Union 
Territories (UTs) based on demand for infrastructure development in the identified areas. 
The proposals recommended by the SLC are considered by the Screening 
Committee(SC) chaired by JS(PMJVK) and then considered and approved by 
Empowered Committee(EC) chaired by Secretary, Ministry of Minority Affairs after due 
consultation with the concerned Central Ministries, projects under PMJVK are 
implemented and managed by concerned State/UT Government/CGOs. 
  
5.3 Education, health, skill development and women-oriented projects are the priority 
sector under PMJVK. The type of works undertaken under PMJVK include construction of 
schools, additional classrooms, hostels, computer labs/digital classrooms, science 
laboratories in schools, drinking water facilities and toilets in schools, colleges, 
dispensaries, hospitals, Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs), Polytechnics, working women 
hostels, sports facilities, public/ community toilets etc. The projects are implemented on a 
fund sharing arrangement between the Centre and the State Government/UT 
Administration in the ratio of 90:10 for North East States, Hilly States (J&K, Himachal 
Pradesh, Uttarakhand)/ UTs without Legislation, 100% for UTs without Legislature and 
60:40 for all other States/ UTs/ UTs with Legislation.   Proposals received from Central 
Government Organisations are supported 100%.

1.5. The Committee, in their original Report, had recommended as follows:- 
“The Committee observe that from 2021-22 to 2023-24, there has been a 
consistent trend of under spending compared to both Revised Estimates 
(RE) and Budget Estimates (BE), with actual expenditures falling short 
across various schemes of the Department. While the Expenditure Finance 
Committee (EFC) has locked both the allocations and physical targets for 
the schemes under the Department, including ADIP, SIPDA, DDRS, and 
Scholarships, for the period from 2021-22 to 2025-26, the Department 
must address the recurring shortfalls in fund utilization. The Committee 
urge the Department to conduct a thorough review of the factors 
contributing to the underutilization of funds and take immediate and 
focused remedial actions. The Committee are also of the opinion that 
proactive engagement with stakeholders is essential to address delays in 
proposal submissions from State Governments, NGOs, and implementing 
agencies, ensuring timely and complete proposals to facilitate smooth fund 
release. Streamlining fund disbursement processes, particularly for skill 
training programs and capital expenditure, is crucial to mitigating delays

meeting the fixed targets for schemes like SIPDA and DDRS, the 
Department should reassess the targets setting to ensure they are realistic

performance trends. Therefore, the Committee recommend that the 
Department should take decisive actions to improve fund utilization and 
achieve the intended outcomes of all the schemes in the remaining years 
of the current financial cycle (2023-2026). This will ensure that the 
resources allocated for the welfare of persons with disabilities are utilized 
effectively, enabling the Department to meet the targets set under various 
Schemes.”

Recommendation (Para No. 6.18) 
The Committee find that while the Central Sector Umbrella Scheme of Scholarship for 
Students with Disabilities has made commendable efforts in empowering students with 
disabilities, several challenges persist in achieving its full potential. The Committee note 
that, despite an increase in budgetary allocations over the years, utilization rates have 
been inconsistent, and physical achievements have fallen short. Challenges such as 
delays in application verifications, insufficient awareness, and technical issues with 
UDID and Aadhaar-based systems have hampered effective implementation. The 
Committee would like to recommend strengthening the verification process at the State 
Nodal Officer level, enhancing the capacity of the National Scholarship Portal to address 
technical bottlenecks, and expanding the scope of outreach programs through targeted 
awareness campaigns. The Committee emphasize the need for timely disbursal of 
funds, regular monitoring through physical inspections, and improved coordination with 
State/UT Governments to reduce pendency and duplication. The Committee further 
recommend revising the scholarship guidelines to ensure adequate flexibility for 
addressing emerging needs and streamlining the documentation process for applicants. 

26 
 
These measures will enhance the effectiveness of the scheme and better serve the 
educational aspirations of students with disabilities. 
  
Reply of the Government 
  
Under the Scholarship Umbrella Scheme, applications are received on NSP online portal 
for the Pre-matric, Post-matric and Top Class Education Scholarship Scheme. Aadhaar 
and UDID have been made mandatory to get the benefits of Scholarships. The Aadhaar 
details of beneficiaries are collected through the National Scholarship 
Portal and Fellowship Management Portal. UDID has also been integrated and 
beneficiary’s information is  fetched through API without any manual intervention for 
correct and accurate data. 
  
The applications are verified at various levels such as from the school or institute level 
to the domicile State or UT level. The State Nodal Officer verifies the application form 
and uploaded documents. The Nodal Officer can verify, defect, reject, or mark the 
application as fake. Once the application is verified at these levels, the National 
Scholarship Portal runs the Sanity checks and generates Red Flags. The doubtful 
applications are again sent to the State Nodal Officers for re-validation. The Department 
releases the scholarship amount only for those applications which are duly verified and 
approved by all verification authorities. The scholarship is disbursed only to the 
Aadhaar-seeded bank account of the beneficiary. Beside of this, the data verification 
works are assigned to the CPMU team for the Post Matric/Top Class Education 
applications and National Fellowship Scholarship Schemes on regular basis. The 
Department has revised the scholarship guideline for the year 2024-25 to ensure 
adequate flexibility for addressing emerging needs and streamlining the documentation 
process for applicants.

of Persons with Disabilities) O.M. No.1/4/2024-25/Budget/DEPwD dated

Recommendation (Para No. 2.18) 
 
The Committee observe that from 2021-22 to 2023-24, there has been a consistent 
trend of under spending compared to both Revised Estimates (RE) and Budget 
Estimates (BE), with actual expenditures falling short across various schemes of the 
Department. While the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) has locked both the 
allocations and physical targets for the schemes under the Department, including ADIP, 
SIPDA, DDRS, and Scholarships, for the period from 2021-22 to 2025-26, the 
Department must address the recurring shortfalls in fund utilization. The Committee 
urge the Department to conduct a thorough review of the factors contributing to the 
underutilization of funds and take immediate and focused remedial actions. The 
Committee are also of the opinion that proactive engagement with stakeholders is 
essential to address delays in proposal submissions from State Governments, NGOs, 
and implementing agencies, ensuring timely and complete proposals to facilitate 
smooth fund release. Streamlining fund disbursement processes, particularly for skill 
training programs and capital expenditure, is crucial to mitigating delays and enhancing 
program delivery. Furthermore, given the challenges in meeting the fixed targets for 
schemes like SIPDA and DDRS, the Department should reassess the targets setting to 
ensure they are realistic and achievable while maintaining flexibility in adjustments 
based on performance trends. Therefore, the Committee recommend that the 
Department should take decisive actions to improve fund utilization and achieve the 
intended outcomes of all the schemes in the remaining years of the current financial 
cycle (2023-2026). This will ensure that the resources allocated for the welfare of 
persons with disabilities are utilized effectively, enabling the Department to meet the 
targets set under various Schemes.

REPORT
I
There is a strong correlation between airports and economic development; while economic growth leads to air
 traffic, increased air traffic necessitates new airports as well as expansion/modernization of existing ones.  The airports
 facilitate the quick and safe movement of men and material giving impetus to trade and tourism.  Airports thus have
 spin-off effect on the surrounding regions in terms of its development and growth.  India has witnessed in recent years
 unprecedented economic growth, but the airport development could not kept pace with this growth. We have seen
 gradual increase not only in the number of aircrafts but also in passenger and cargo traffic.   In the years 2002-03, 2003-
04, and 2004-05 the aircraft movement at the 126 airports managed by the Airports Authority of India increased by
 10%, 13.5% and 12.6% respectively, passenger movement by 9.96% , 10.69% and 21.6% respectively and cargo
 movement by 15%, 18.75% and 19.9% respectively. As a result, several major airports still remain congested offering
 slow and inefficient services.
Modernization of Airports
2.         Being aware of such a demand being generated in this sector, the Government of India decided to modernize and
 expand its airports in the country. It constituted a high-powered ‘Committee on Infrastructure’ under the Prime Minister
 on the 31
st August 2004, to initiate policy measures to ensure creation of world-class infrastructure in a time-bound
 manner. This work being highly capital intensive as it is, suitable policy and regulatory framework for Public Private
 Partnership (PPP) was also thought for maximizing capital inflows and efficiency.  The Committee on Infrastructure
 (CoI) in its meeting held on the 10 th December 2004, decided that a framework for airport development up to 2010
 would be planned, assuming an annual traffic growth at 16 per cent.   In the third meeting of the Empowered Sub-
committee of the CoI held on 3 rd October, 2005, it was decided to set up a Task Force headed by a Member, Planning
 Commission and comprising representatives of Ministry of Civil Aviation, Department of Economic Affairs,
 Department of Expenditure, and Airports Authority of India to deliberate and submit a financing plan for the
 development of airports, and for upgrading and augmenting the airport infrastructure in India.  The Task Force held
 meetings on the 7
th November, 2005, 6 th January, 2006, 27 th March, 2006 and 5 th May, 2006 to formulate its
 recommendations.  The report of the Task Force was discussed by the Empowered Sub-committee of CoI in its meeting
 held on 9th June, 2006 and approved with some modifications, which were being incorporated in the financing plan.
3.         The Task Force recommended that Metro airports and Greenfield airports have to be developed through the
 Public Private Partnerships (PPPs) mode.  However, the modalities in respect of Kolkata and Chennai airports were left
 to be decided after further consultations.
4.         Accordingly, airports in Delhi and Mumbai are being developed through the PPP.  Bengaluru and Hyderabad
 Greenfield Airports developed in this mode are already functional.   
5.         The Ministry of Civil Aviation proposed development of 35 non-metro airports keeping in view the potential for
 traffic, tourism, business etc.  The development of these airports was proposed under three heads namely; (a) terminal
 building, cargo parking and cargo; (b) airside; and (c) cityside (cargo complexes, hotels and flight kitchens).   Airports
 Authority of India had proposed that the capital investment for commercial exploitation and development of land
 (cityside development) of non-metro airports would be made by private participation.   It was also proposed that out of
 their commercial revenues, private partners would pay land lease and revenue share to Airports Authority of India.  The
 proposed commercial exploitation would be restricted to cargo complexes, hotels, flight kitchens and parking could
 also be included, if necessary. 
6.         In the light of the considerations spelt out above, the Task Force on financing plan for airports recommended on

Modernisation of Mumbai and Delhi airports
8.         The Cabinet in its meeting held on the 11th September, 2003 accorded its approval for the restructuring of Delhi
 and Mumbai airports by adopting the joint venture route.  The AAI (Amendment) Bill, was passed in June 2003 which
 authorized AAI to transfer the operations and management of its airports by way of long-term lease to private players. 
 The Cabinet constituted an Empowered Group of Ministers (EGoM) to take decisions on various issues connected with
 restructuring of Mumbai and Delhi airports.  In this connection, the Cabinet also decided to constitute an Inter
 Ministerial Group (IMG) to assist EGoM.  In this Joint Venture, the Airports Authority of India and other Government
 PSUs held 26% equity, with the balance 74% held by the strategic partners.  The Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in
 this transaction has been kept at 49%.  On the basis of the evaluation of technical and financial bids, it was decided by
 the Government on the 1
st February, 2006 that GMR consortium and GVK Consortium would be the private partner for
 modernization and development of Delhi and Mumbai airports respectively.
Modernization of Mumbai airport
9.         Mumbai International Airport Pvt. Ltd. (MIAL) a Joint Venture Company (JVC) of Airports Authority of India
 (AAI) (26%) and GVK Led Consortium (74%) took over management and development of Chhatrapati Shivaji
 International Airport (CSIA) w.e.f. 3 rd May, 2006.  There was transition phase of three months and w.e.f. 3 rd August,
 2006, MIAL is independently handling management and operation of CSIA.
10.       As per the Master plan prepared by MIAL, total project cost for development of CSIA is estimated to be Rs.9800
 crores.  Till 31st March 2008, MIAL has spent Rs.937 crores.  Estimated capital expenditure till 31st March 2009 would
 be Rs.3081 crores.  Financial closure for the project was achieved on 24th April, 2007.
11.       Operation, Management and Development Agreement (OMDA) which was signed on 4 th April 2006 prescribe
 that mandatory capital projects to be completed as per schedule 7.  It also lists out various compliances and procedures
 to be followed.  It also spells out subjective and objective service quality requirements to be achieved by MIAL.
 OMDA prescribes objective service quality standard (schedule 3) and subjective quality standard (schedule 4).  These
 standards are being achieved.   In the survey conducted by Airport Council International (ACI) for the quarter ending
 the 31st December, 2007, Mumbai airport has been rated at 3.58 on a scale of 0-5, which is highest among all Indian
 airports.  CSI Airport has also been granted ISO 10002:2004 certification. As per schedule 7 of OMDA, there are 32

Observations and Recommendations of the Committee
53.       The Committee on Infrastructure headed by the Prime Minister at its 12 th meeting on the 8 th June 2006
 decided that for 35 non-metro airports, the Airports Authority of India will undertake the airport side
 development, including terminal building, while the cityside development will be undertaken through  private
 public partnership.  However, the Committee has been given to understand that the Inter Ministerial Group
 headed by Secretary Civil Aviation has decided on 6 May 2008, to deviate from  the decision taken by the
 Committee on Infrastructure headed by the Prime Minster.  Now the IMG has suggested that the commercial
 operations in the terminal building will be done through PPP.   The IMG decided that the scope of work of the
 project would include commercial operation and maintenance of Terminal  Building, development and
 operatrion of Cargo and real estate development on the land identified for the purpose.  Maintenance of the
 Terminal Building would include maintenance of the building, equipment and utilities. On the basis of this
 decision, the Planning Commission has prepared a Model Concession Agreement for PPP for 30 years for
 terminal buildings. 
54.       The Committee feels that this is a deviation from the decision of the Committee on Infrastructure and fails
 to understand how the IMG headed by the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation, can go against or deviate from
 the decisions/directions of the COI headed by the Prime Minister himself.  The Committee, therefore, expects 
 PMO to issue a clarification in this regard, if the IMG had its approval for deviating from the CoI and if not, it
 must intervene in this matter to ensure that the commercial operation of terminal buildings was done by the
 Airports Authority of India itself. 
55.       Commercial operation of terminal buildings is a profit making activity which would have generate
 revenue for the Airports Authority of India to spend on developing airside operations.
56.       The Committee, therefore, recommends that the airport side development including the commercial use of
 terminal building should be entrusted to the Airport Authority of India.  The AAI is also of the view that there
 will be conflict of interests, if private parties and AAI were involved into this simultaneously. 
57.       The Airports Authority of India that has been continuously earning profit every year and has proven
 ability of setting up, maintaining and modernizing airports in India and also abroad.   Even the private Cochin
 International Airport had been developed by it.  The Committee is, therefore, against the handing-over of the
 profit making airports to the private sector in the name of modernization and reconstruction, specially when the
 Airports Authority of India possesses the proven capability for this task.
58.       The Committee also learnt that the Government was planning to hand over 15 more profit making
 airports to private parties in the name of constructing green field airports.
59.       The Committee notes that the greenfield airports that are proposed to be handed over to private parties
 are largely being financed by Airports Authority of India, concerned State Governments and also by Indian
 Financial Institutions.   The Committee wonders, if the private players can manage the necessary resources
 within India, why can’t the Airports Authority of India be allowed to pursue the same business strategy.  In
 2006, when the Delhi and Mumbai Airports were being allowed to be modernized/expanded through PPP mode,
 the Airports Authority of India had submitted a plan with lesser time frame for the modernization of these
 airports.  However, these were turned down for unknown reasons.  The Committee feels that had the
 Government agreed to this proposal of the Airports Authority of India, the Mumbai and Delhi Airports would

Airport Modernisation
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/141threport.htm[28-08-2018 13:34:41]
 have been completed by this time.  The Committee does not agree to the Government’s logic that the
 modernization of airports can be done only through privatization. It is a wrong and misplaced assumption.  
 Airports, assuming important role in our economy as they are, the Committee feels, must be under strong public
 regulation, if not under direct public control to ensure that unfair monopolistic practices do not become
 rampant.  Internationally, most successful examples of airport management are known to have retained over all
 public control even while outsourcing some particular activities to private people.  For example, many airports
 have successfully brought in private parties to invest in cargo handling facilities, parking bays, servicing and
 overhauling facilities, maintaining terminals and so on.  However, in India we are handing over the entire
 airport to the private parties which are in total negation to the best practices available in the world. 
60.       The representatives of the Planning Commission who appeared before the Committee submitted that the
 Committee on Infrastructure decided that for Kolkota Airport planning for terminals should be undertaken on
 a modular basis whereas the Airport Authority of India had planned a big ‘L’  shape terminal.   AAI was
 planning to build a capacity which is for four times the present traffic.  The Planning Commission opined that if
 the Airports Authority of India were to make a very huge investment today, it will inevitably lead to much
 higher user charges.  They were not ready to accept a situation where air fares are coming down but airport
 charges are going up.   When the Committee enquired if the same logic applied to the Hyderabad and Bengaluru
 Airports, the representatives of the Planning Commission were evasive by stating that the Planning Commission
 did not discuss that matter.   The Committee also notes the assurance given to the Committee by the Chairman
 AAI that in Kolkata airport it did not propose to charge any user development fees from the passengers.
61.       The committee has learnt that the newly opened Bengaluru and Hyderabad Greenfield airports are
 reported to have faced decline in short-haul passenger traffic due to the fact that the passengers have to travel a
 long distance to reach the airports.  The short-haul passengers are opting for other modes of transport like train
 and road journey.  The Committee, therefore, would like to draw the attention of the Government to the
 recommendation contained in its 131
st Report wherein the Committee inter-alia has recommended that the old
 airports at Bengaluru and Hyderabad airports should be made operational.  The Action Taken Report from the
 Government, however, is awaited.
62.       Meanwhile, the Committee came to know that the Ministry of Civil Aviation asked the BIAL to make
 arrangements to increase its capacity in the next eighth months as the construction of the second terminal would
 take three years.  It would, therefore be a better option to augment the capacity by restarting the functioning of
 existing HAL airport.  In order to ensure that the wide winged aircraft be accommodated properly at the
 Greenfield airports, the Government can take a policy decision to allow the small aircraft and ATRs to operate
 from the existing airports.  The Committee, therefore, once again calls upon the Ministry of civil Aviation to
 take necessary steps to ensure that the existing airports at Hyderabad and Bengaluru are kept functional. 
63.       The Committee notes that this approach of the Planning Commission and the Government was
 privatizing terminal buildings and other airport operations that were being managed, hitherto, by the Airports
 Authority of India, was knowingly or unknowingly, benefiting the private agencies.  The Committee is
 constrained to say that the Government and the Planning Commission appear to be least concerned about
 passenger comfort and the operational efficiency of the airports.  The Committee strongly recommends that
 while modernising the airports, care should be taken not to involve multiple agencies for maintenance and
 operations of the terminal building.  The Committee is of the view that the leading airport infrastructure
 provider, the Airports Authority of India, should have a better say in the modernization of airports in the
 country.  Any further move to offer the airport terminals to the private persons through PPP mode will
 definitely affect the profits as well as the morale of a premier organization like the Airports Authority of India. 
 Another problem would be the fate of the people working in the organization.  More than 80% of the employees
 of Airports Authority of India in Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad are waiting for their transfer to
 some other places due to privatization of these airports, and only a few of them have decided to join the Joint
 Venture Companies.  Though the lease of terminals in the non-metro airports on PPP mode may fill the coffers
 of Government, it will definitely make a negative impact on the employees of AAI.   
64.       The Committee notes the statement made by the representatives of the Ministry of Civil Aviation that a
 decision on handing over the terminal buildings in non-metro airports to private parties had not been finalized
 so far.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in view of economy of scale, operational convenience and as

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to submit on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred Forty Second Report on Functioning of Private Airports and related
issues.
2. The Government of India had decided to modernize and upgrade the existing domestic and
international airports at Mumbai and Delhi to world standards and to construct Greenfield airports
in Bangalore and Hyderabad through Public Private Partnership. The Greenfield airports in
Hyderabad and Bangalore have started functioning from the 23rd March and 24th May, 2008
respectively. The modernization of Delhi and Mumbai Airports are in different stages of
development.
3. There were a large number of reports/representations about the problems faced by the
passengers and associated agencies at Mumbai and Delhi Airports and also at Bengaluru and
Hyderabad after the new Greenfield airports were opened and the old ones were closed. The
Committee while discussing these issues felt it necessary to visit these airports for an on-the-
spot assessment of the problems and to see facilities available at these airports. Accordingly,
the Committee visited the new airports at Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Mumbai from the 14th to
20th September, 2008 on this issue. The Committee also visited the old airport at Begumpet, in
Hyderabad. The Committee had already visited the Delhi Airport on l0th January, 2008. The
Committee interacted with various stakeholders at these airports for finalizing its report.
4. Apart from passenger amenities, the Committee has also dealt with various issues/points
relating to the policy of privatization of airports, procedures adopted for this and other related
matters.
5. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the representatives of the Ministry of Civil
Aviation, Airports Authority of India, managements of Bangalore International Airport Ltd. (BIAL),
Hyderabad International Airport Ltd. (HIAL), Mumbai International Airport Ltd. (MIAL) and Delhi
International Airport Ltd. (DIAL) for placing before the Committee the material and information
desired in connection with the subject and for clarifying the points raised by the Members.
6. The committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the
20th October, 2008.
SITARAM YECHURY
N

Asvina 28, 1930  (Saka) Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture.

1
REPORT
India is experiencing a phenomenal growth in its aviation sector which plays a vital role in
the overall economic growth of the country. The Indian civil aviation sector has shown an
extraordinary growth rate in the last few years. In 2006-07, total air passenger traffic increased
by 32.6% with around 78.7 million passengers, of whom 57.5 million reflecting an increase of
40.5% were domestic passengers and 21.2 million showing an increase of 15% in international
sector. Present slackness in aviation sector both national and international, notwithstanding, the air
passenger traffic is expected to grow in the coming years.
2. Presently, India has a total of 454 airports or airstrips including operational, non-operational,
abandoned and unused airports, of which 138 belong to India’s defence establishment, 97 to
Airports Authority of India (AAI), 158 to various State Governments, and 61 to its fledgling private
sector. Due to increase in traffic both domestic and international, movement of aircrafts has also
gone up rapidly. However, such a growth in air traffic has led to strain on the available aviation
infrastructure, which is already over-stretched. It has resulted in traffic congestions and delays
mainly at the major airports. To sustain this boom in the civil aviation sector, an urgent need for
expansion and improvement of the airport infrastructure was felt to cope up with the emerging
requirements. Airports being the centres of economic activity, play a crucial role in the Nation’s
economy. Faced with. such a situation, the Government is working on a proposal of getting around
500 airports operational by 2020, which would include redevelopment of currently unused airports,
Greenfield airports, and also ‘merchant’ airports dedicated to the movement of cargo and logistics.
It is estimated that by 2020, Indian airports should be able to handle 100 million passengers
including 60 million domestic passengers and cargo in the range of 3.4 million tones per annum.
3. The Government decided to modernize and upgrade some for the existing domestic and
international airports to world standards. The Government through its Airport Infrastructure Policy
of 1997, decided to set up Greenfield Airports in the country. As a result, permission was granted
to construct two Greenfield Airports at Devanahalli in Bengaluru and Shamshabad in Hyderabad on
joint venture basis in PPP mode. The selected companies, namely, GMR Hyderabad International
Airport Ltd. (GHIAL); and Bengaluru International Airport Ltd. (BIAL) entered into Concession
Agreements separately with the Government of India for development, construction operation and
maintenance of the Airports at these places. Both these airports have started functioning from 2008.
The Government also handed over the Delhi and Mumbai airports to the Joint Venture Companies
namely, GMR and GVK groups respectively for modernization. The modernization of these airports
is in different stages of development.
4. There were a large number of reports/representations about the problems faced by the
passengers and associated agencies at Mumbai and Delhi Airports and also at Bengaluru and
Hyderabad after the new Greenfield airports were opened and the old ones were closed. The
Committee while discussing these Issues felt it necessary to visit these private airports for an on-
the-spot assessment of the problems and to see facilities available at these airports.
5. The Committee, accordingly, visited new airports at Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Mumbai
from the 14th to 20th September, 2008. The Committee also visited the old Begumpet airport at
Hyderabad. The Committee had taken stock of the facilities, available and proposed, as also the
problems being faced by the passengers/tourist, Airports Authority of India (AAI), Private Airline
operators and other associated agencies at these airports. The Committee also discussed the issues
at length with the representatives of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, Airports Authority of India,
CEOs of BIAL, HIAL and MIAL, Airports Authority Employees Unions and Private Airlines.

2
Operators. During its visit, the Committee had also received a large number of written
representations from various stakeholders.
(A) Bengaluru International Airport Limited (BIAL)
6. The Committee has been informed that the BIAL is being developed to handle upto 11
million passengers as Greenfield airport at Devanahalli near Bengaluru on a Build Operate and
Transfer (BOT) basis with Public Private Participation. Government of Karnataka through Karnataka
State Industrial Investment Development Corporation (KSIIDC) and AAI each hold 13% equity and
the strategic joint venture partners hold the balance 74%. A Memorandum of Understandlng to this
effect was signed on the 3rd May 1999, between AAI and KSIIDC to facilitate further action
leading to implementation of the project.
7. A consortium led by Siemens, Germany with Unique Zurich, Switzerland and Larsen and
Toubro India Ltd. as other members, have been chosen as the strategic Joint Venture Partners.
Government of Karnataka is extending Rs.3.5 billon as State support and is providing approximately
4000 acres of land on concessional rate. AAI’s investment in the equity is capped at Rs. 50 crore,
while the approximate cost of the project is Rs. 1400 crore.
8. While the construction of the new airport commenced on the 2nd July, 2005, it started its
operations from the 24th May; 2008.
9. During the course of discussions, the representatives of BIAL informed the Committee that
the project implementation of BIAL has been done with thrust on predominant use of locally
available input materials. Meticulous supervision and stringent quality control were enforced during
project implementation. In the Phase-I of the Project Implementation, BIAL has constructed the
following facilities:
(a) Operational Facilities: This airport currently has Runway which is 4000 mts. long and 60 mts.
wide with 6 exits. It has 9 Aerobridges, 8 one armed and 1 double armed. There are 42 Aircrafts
stands (Code C aircraft stands). It provides 13 Security counters (8 Domestic and 5 International)
and has five level security screening system for checked-in baggage. Immigration Counters are 18,
both departure and arrival. It has a Cargo Capacity of 350,000 tons annually (presently
160,000.tons).
(b) Terminal building Facilities: This airport has 53 check-in counters including 18 self check-
in counters. It has single check-in process with no queues for screening baggage. Various facilities
like Valet Service, Shops, restaurants and lounges (common & dedicated), Short walkways, Baby
care, 24 hour pharmacy, Special needs-elevators with Braille Plates and Free Wi-Fi access have also
been provided at this airport.
Buses: 46 V ayu Vajra AC V olvo buses and 23 Suvara non AC buses are run for airport shuttle
service having minimum fare of Rs.70 and Maximum of Rs.200 for AC buses and Rs.20 to 90 for
non-AC buses.
Taxi: AC Taxi Services- Merucabs and Easycabs, equipped with tracking service are also being run.
Post paid taxis are available on meter charges @Rs.15/-per km. Cars can be rented for self drive-
a new concept at an Indian airport
Car parking arrangements: Airport has a car parking with 2000 car park slots, in which 700
car park slots are for employees. Charges are: for the first 10 minutes free, Rs.40/- for 2 hours
and Rs.20 per additional hour, Rs.300 for 24 hrs with Rs.200 for every additional day. Porter
services are there for minimum Rs.70 for up to 3 bags and V alet service is for Rs.150.
Helicopter: Deccan Aviations helicopter shuttle service has provided 3 pick up points - Electronic
city, Whitefield, Palace grounds and HAL, operating between 630 hours to 1800 hours. Minimum

3
fare is Rs.4800/- and maximum fare is Rs.5800/- per person per trip. New Service by Global
Vectra heli services will begin in October, 2008.
Travel retail unlocked
• Airport has a design reflecting the flowers of Lal Bagh. It has a mix of domestic and
international brands in 18 shopping outlets to choose from. It has Duty Free Shops at
arrival and departure areas and 15 Food and Beverages outlets ranging from local cuisine
to international cafes. It has 2 Lounges and another 2 more in the making. Additional
reserved lounge are being created.
• It had handled 2.5 million passengers as on August 29, 2008, with 30,000 air craft
movements and 45,000 MT of cargo. It has seen 30% increase in international flights.
BIAL has approx.5000 employees.
• It claimed 70% increase in the toilets and increase in passenger seating areas and seats
and has installed drinking water fountains.
• It handled on an average 151 arrival/departure flights per day with departure of 9431
domestic passengers and departure of 2283 international passengers per day.
• Average arrival of domestic passengers per day is 9330 and of international passengers
per day was 2279.
Extension Plan
Phase – 1:  The BIAL extension plan has been design to expand and upgrade infrastructure of the
Initial Project, Re-design 2006, Trumpet Fly-over, Airline Buildings, Greenery and canopy and
Security Equipment PSF.
Phase – 2:  This phase is the implementation of several immediate measures such as Apron
Expansion and Express Terminal
Phase – 3:  Phase 3 to be completed by 2012 includes Terminal 2 and Second runway
(B) Hyderabad International Airport Limited (HIAL)
10. HIAL also is a public-private joint venture between GMR Group, Malaysia Airports Holdings
Berhad and the State Government of Andhra Pradesh and Airports Authority of India (AAI). The
Greenfield airport at Shamshabad near Hyderabad is being implemented on a Build Operate and
Transfer (BOT) basis with Public Private Participation. The Government of Andhra Pradesh (GoAP)
have selected a consortium led by M/s GMR as the developer for this airport. The Government
of Andhra Pradesh and AAI together hold 26% equity, with AAI’s investment in the equity capped
at Rs.50 crore. The joint venture partners, GMR Group holds the balance 74% in the Company
namely, Hyderabad International Airport Ltd. (HIAL) set up to implement the project. The
Government of Andhra, Pradesh extended Rs.315 crore as State support and Rs.107 crore as, a
grant. Further, Government of Andhra Pradesh provided 5000 acres of land on concessional rate.
The concession Agreement between the GoI and HIAL was executed on the 20th December 2004.
11. The Committee visited the Shamshabad airport on the 17th September, 2008 and was
informed that the total project cost, as per the DPR submitted by HIAL, was estimated to be
Rs.I400 crore (2005 figure). This was being financed by State support to the extent of
Rs.422 crore and rest by way of Debt and Equity to the tune of 40% and 60%, respectively. This
project cost was for estimated passenger traffic of 5 million. However, the final cost of the project
is Rs.2920 crore for estimated passenger traffic of 12 million. The new airport started its
operations from the 23rd March, 2008.

4
12. During the course of the discussion with the Committee, the representative of HIAL
presented the following facts about the passenger amenities available at the airport:
Location: Airport is located at 25Km/I9 miles from Begumpet, the old airport. It is operating 22
airlines connecting 35 destinations which is further growing. Total area of the project is 5495
acres.
Airport Capacity:  It has initial passenger capacity of 12 million persons per annum (MPPA), with
the ultimate capacity of over 40, MPPA. Initial car go capacity is l 1akh MT/Per Annum (MTPA)
and final capacity would be 1.3 million, MTPA. It has an exclusive cargo apron for four, code C
freighter aircraft with facility for “Express/Courier’ cargo.
Operational facilities: It has India’s longest runway (4.2 km) which is A 380 Compatible and has
India’s longest taxiway (4.2 km). Airport has 10 runway entry/exit points (including four rapid exit
taxiways).
Car Parking arrangements:  It has parking area for 3000 cars in front of passenger terminal
building providing easy Transit from domestic to international and vice-versa.
Terminal building facilities: It has 130 Check-in-counters with CUTE (Common User Terminal
Equipment) and 16 self check-in kiosks with CUSS (Common User Self Service).
• 46 Immigration counters - 23 departure and 22 arrival and 1 transit. . City Check-in
facility has been proposed at Begumpet and Secunderabad Railway Stations. There are
42 aircraft parking stands including 12 passenger boarding bridges.
• It uses modem IT systems like FIDS (Flight Information Display Systems), ACN
(Airport Community Network), Baggage Tag & Boarding Card Printers etc. It claimed
to have tallest A TC Tower (75 mtr.).
• The Committee was informed that the Airport has a full fledged medical center,
international brand concessionaires, radio taxis system and Aero express shuttle services.
A business hotel with 308 rooms is also coming up.
• For security, 4 level in-line baggage security system has been put in place with
perimeter intrusion detection system.
• The airport had completed 178 days of operation and handled 3.10 million passengers,
with average daily ATMs of 240. it also claimed that ATF Sales had increased from 550
KL/day as compared to old Begumpet airport to around 880 KL/day now.
• GMR management claimed to have taken feedback/suggestions from 1.5 lakh passengers
and other stakeholders till date and had incorporated these inputs to improve the
services further and increase passenger convenience.
13. The Committee found the plan and design of the Greenfield airports to be of the
international standard with certain useful facilities for the comfort and convenience of the
passengers, for example, adequate and efficient check-in counters, self check-in machines
and quick immigration clearance, large number of shops, eateries, etc. However, the
Committee also came across certain areas that needed immediate attention. For example,
the Committee found that the passengers at the Greenfield airports have to pay exorbitant
prices for food items. The eateries are charging much more than the MRP, which is against
the Supreme Court order. There is no separate canteen for the employees and the staff
working at the airports. The drivers and others who are waiting outside the airports have
no affordable canteen facility and basic amenities like toilets and bathrooms. The
Committee recommends that the Government should ensure that the Greenfield Airports at

5
Bengaluru and Hyderabad provide basic facilities to the drivers and passengers and stop the
eateries from charging exorbitant prices. Private airlines have to cough up hefty amounts
for parking bays and aerobridges, security charges, lounge rentals, telephone rentals and
other facilities at the new airports.
14. The parking charges for vehicles are also quite heavy at the new airports. At
Bengaluru, it is Rs.40/- per hour and Rs.20/-per additional hours. The Committee is
surprised to know that at Hyderabad airport, a vehicle while entering the airport for
dropping or picking up a passenger has to pay Rs.35/- per trip. The Committee notes that
space earmarked for passenger seating areas was inadequate and numbers of seats are also
not adequate, causing inconvenience to the passengers during peak times. This is so because
much of the airport space has been let out for commercial use and given to shopping outlets
and F&B outlets. There is conspicuous absence of lounges at these airports. There is a need
for creation of additional reserved lounge for VIPs and passengers. To help and guide the
passengers at these airports, there should be round-the-clock help service at these airports.
There were inadequate facilities provided for free drinking water at these airports. More
drinking water fountains should be installed. The emergency medical facilities for treatment
of the passengers in case of sudden illness should be in place in all the new airports as has
been done at the new Hyderabad airport.
15. The Committee recommends that the flight delay or cancellation must be reported
to passengers well in time to avoid hardships to the passengers. The baggage handling
process should be strengthened so as to reduce the baggage delivery time and hardship to
the passengers. Apron driving discipline should be maintained to avoid any accident on
apron and staff should be given proper training for the driving skills and behaviours. There
should be integration of air and ground surveillance information along with flight related
data to enhance air. travel safety and efficient air traffic management.
16. The private operators should recognize various staff welfare committees of Airports
Authority of India and others working at these airports. There should be regular
consultative and coordination meeting of all the stakeholders at the new airports so as to
resolve the different issues/grievances.
17. The Committee learnt that it was discouraging for the short-haul passengers to take
air travel after the new airports. A higher User Development Fee (UDF) was being charged
by the new airport developers from the passengers. The user development fee added with
high taxi/bus fares due to long distances, compel the passengers to use other means of
transport such as road and trains for the short distance destinations. This has, in fact
rendered the air travel from these airports added with high ATF prices, just prohibitive.
18. The Committee notes that the Task force on Financing Plan for airports (July 2006)
had recommended that the users should not be burdened with ADF/UDF for financing at the
airport projects. This is particularly important in the context of the policy objective to make
civil aviation a mass, rather than an elitist model of travel and to make air travel more
affordable. After taking into account various aspects and the above recommendation of the
Task Force the committee feels that the imposition of UDF on passengers is a retrograde
step contravening the Task Force recommendations and recommends that the UDF imposed
on passengers may be withdrawn immediately and no more UDF may be imposed on
passengers in any of the airports.
19. CAPACITY OF BIAL AIRPORT
19.1 As per the original Concession Agreement (CA) dated 05.07.2004, BIAL was supposed to

6
build a Terminal of 55,000 sq. mtr. to accommodate 2017 passengers in the peak hour. This works
out to annual capacity of around 4.00 million passengers. The Committee was informed that the
CA was amended in 2006 and the capacity of the airport was enhanced to 2733 passengers during
peak hour with a terminal capacity of 71500 sq. m.
19.2 However, the current terminal is of total 71310 sq. m., out of which the basement area
consists of around 18665 sq. m. The basement area is neither used, nor usable by the passengers.
This space is used for storage, services and utilities. Hence, this cannot be counted while
computing the total terminal area. Also the kerb area of 5616 sq m outside the terminal which is
not a part of the terminal building and not used by passengers.
19.3 As per the IATA guidelines, the type of airport (level C) the area per peak hour passenger
(PHP) should be 26 sq m per passenger. As per the Concession Agreement, the area per passenger
should be 27.3 sq m. Hence, considering the actual terminal area available for passengers, the
capacity of the terminal works out to be 1928 PHP only, against the 2733 PHP capacity to be
provided as per the Concession Agreement.
19.4 As per the IATA standards, the area required for 10 million passengers per annum is 150000
sq. m. In view of the above, it can be inferred that the actual capacity of the BIAL terminal
building is still around 3.5 million only (1928 passengers per peak hour), which is much below the
capacity to be provided by BIAL as per the Concession Agreement.
19.5 BIAL was obligated to provide the facilities as per the IATA/ICAO standards. As per the
IATA standards the maximum commercial area permissible in the. terminal area is 12% of the total
passenger area. But in case of BIAL, 30% of terminal space has been utilised for commercial area.
If this aspect is considered the capacity of the terminal would further come down.
19.6 The Committee notes that the Government of India appears to be unconcerned about
the obligation of BIAL to construct and provide an airport as per the concession agreement.
Even the area and capacity were not verified before permitting to open new and closing HAL
Airport. This appears to be an irregularity committed by Government of India in this
matter.
20. During the meeting at Hyderabad the representatives of the AAEU argued that the idea
behind developing the Greenfield Airport was to handle the excess traffic beyond the capacity of
existing Airports. But, in this case, the entire commercial operations were diverted and old airport
was closed for commercial operation. This has deprived Airports Authority of India a huge revenue.
The Committee was informed that Begumpet Airport is having the full fledged infrastructure for
efficient operation of NTR Domestic Terminal/Rajiv Gandhi International Terminal. This airport has
handled wide bodied aircrafts defence/commercial/cargo airlines of various countries. Recently AAI
have spent roughly Rs.200 crore towards development of infrastructure of Begumpet Airport with
a commitment to serve to the public for another fifteen years. Presently the entire establishment
worth thousands of crores is lying idle.
21. Before commissioning of the Greenfield Airport, the airport at Hyderabad was the sixth
largest airport in India having 250 scheduled aircraft movements per day. 10 domestic and 13
international operators operated from this Airport. In 2006-07, a total of 69727 aircraft movement
was registered with the 5.87 millions passengers. In 2007-08, a total of 86484 aircrafts movements
were registered with 7.05 millions passengers. After commissioning of the new airports the old
airport is catering only to VVIP aircrafts, defence movement, local flying club, and movement
related to emergencies and general aviation including chartered aircrafts.
22. The Committee wanted to know the details of flights which were handled at old Hyderabad
Airport after its closure for commercial operations and RNFC collected by the Airports Authority

7
of India. The Committee was informed that a total number of 631 movements of Airforce Aircrafts
and 654 take off was done since the closure of airport till 5th July, 2008. As regard total number
of movement of private, non-commercial, non-revenue and VIP flights including helicopters was
478 landings and 479 take offs upto 5th September, 2008. The RNFC collected for casual flight
operations since March, 2008 is Rs.1,72,498.00. The Committee was informed that the short haul
traffic growth has been reduced after the opening of the new airports at Bengaluru and Hyderabad.
The Aircraft movements per day from HAL Airport as on 23.05.08 were 361 whereas the aircraft
movement per day from HIAL as on 1st week of September, 2008 was 280.
23. It was also submitted before the Committee that Airports Authority of India with
comprehensive traffic study/survey can distribute the traffic for both the Airports on competitive
basis based on the handling capacity, peak load traffic on operative measurement basis with the
available infrastructure from the existing operating airport (Begumpet) comparing with Shamshabad
Airport, since the funnel point for both the airports are same with regard to traffic movement.
After commissioning the new Greenfield Airport by the private operator the practical difficulties for
the passengers and airline operators have increased enormously on various account such as road
travel, UDF, etc. which affects the air travelers very badly and the very purpose of low cost
airlines will be defeated. Therefore, the decision to close down the existing airport within the
frame-work of concession agreement needs to be reviewed immediately.
24. The Committee notes that hundreds of crores of rupees were spent for developing
infrastructure at the old airports at Bengaluru and Hyderabad but it is lying unutilized due
to the closure of airports for commercial purposes. Another interesting thing brought to the
notice of the Committee is that the old airports, the HAL Airport and Begumpet airport,
are being used for operation of VIP flights, Non-schedule Flights, General Aviation,
Helicopter-Taxis, etc. During the deliberations of the Committee the Airports Authority of
India reported that there is absolutely no problem in opening up two airports
simultaneously in a city. The Committee therefore, recommends that the old airports of
Hyderabad and Bengaluru may be used exclusively for short haul flights which are operating
from the nearby airports.
25. The Committee also notes that the closure of HAL airport led to loss of jobs due to
reduction of flights and due to closure of airlines operators. Thousands of direct and indirect
workers also lost their jobs, this also includes trolley retrievers, small time vendors, taxi
drivers, auto drivers, loaders etc. Despite the assurances given by the BIAL and HIAL
managements, they have not been accommodated in the new airports. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that all those people who are directly or indirectly affected due to
closure of the HAL Airport and Begumpet Airport may be given preference and suitably
accommodated at the new Green Field Airports.
26. The Committee is of the opinion that the HAL Airport is most convenient for
common public due to it being situated closer to the City Centre, easy accessibility and
availability of multi-mode transport options like Bus, Auto, Taxis, even 2-wheeler, etc. HAL
Airport, therefore, would be more convenient and economical for public compared to BIAL
due to absence of UDF and less transportation cost due to multiple modes and shorter
distance. Less time in coming and going from the airport is also important aspect in this
regard.
27. The Committee further recommends that the old airports may be made operational
for short-haul passengers. Moreover, this is the practice being followed in many of the
major cities in the world wherein more than one airport exists. There is no reason or
justification for keeping the hundreds of crores of worth infrastructure at the old airports
idle just to be used for VIP and other flights.
