Jawaharlal Nehru Port
191. The Committee was informed that the road leading to the Jawaharlal Nehru Port handles
approximately 4.5 million TUEs of container cargo, 6.49 million tonnes of liquid and 1.5 million
tonnes of other cargo. For improving road connectivity, the Port has formed a SPV with NHAI

35
and CIDCO at an estimated cost of Rs.357 crores and about 95% work is completed. Mumbai-
JNPT road, Mumbai-Goa Highway (NH-17) widening of the NH-4B to four lane and the SH-54 are
the major works to be completed that would benefit the cargo movements in the port. Some issues
related to the land acquisition is to be cleared.
192. The Committee was also informed that the Port is planning for a Centralized parking plaza
for export containers which will have single window clearance system. The plaza will be of around
46 ha. area and the investment is around Rs.122 crores.
193. The Committee was informed that the Port is planning a Port Based Multi Product SEZ in
an area of 277 hectare on the Port land as Phase-1 development with an approximate investment
of Rs.3,500 crores on PPP basis. The Project has received ‘in principle’ approval of Ministry of
Commerce and Ministry of Shipping and the RFQ document is observed of the awaiting approval
of the Ministry of Shipping.
Kandla Port
194. Kandla Port Trust has taken up the work of four lane road from National Highway to Oil
Jetty Complex and it is nearing completion. Two- lane road constructed from National Highway
8-A to Tuna Port will be widened to four-lane. The Committee was informed that road from berth
No. 11 to 16 at Kandla, the road up to 12
th cargo berth has been completed and road network up
to berth no.16 th will be developed shortly. Kandla Port Trust has requested NHAI to widen four-
lane road connectivity from Gandhidham to Kandla (15 kms.) from four-lane to six-lane. The NHAI
was requested to construct the road above 5 km. before the Railway Crossing directly connecting
National Highway at village Mithirohar. At Tagore Road, Gandhidham, NHAI was further requested
to construct a parallel road from national highway 8-A near KASEZ to Village Antarjal Road leading
to Vadinar Dwarka-Jamnagar road and it is proposed to be widened for better connectivity to
Vadinar.

to be widened from 4-lane to 6-lane while a mere 8 km. length connecting the Kandla Port has
been left behind. Even though the cost of the work will be not so high the actual benefit will be
marry fold. A road link from NH 8-A near KESEZ to State highway near village Atanjal shall reduce
the congestion of Tagore Road connecting Adipur-Gandhidham township. This will improve the
cargo movement from the Port. The feasibility report has been got prepared for road connecting
Vadinar with cargo berths, oil jetties, bunkering facilities, ship repairs, off shore facilities etc. This
plan has to be materialized for future development needs.
New Mangalore Port
196. The New Mangalore Port’s gate is directly connected to the NH-17, which is currently
being upgraded to 4-lane highway from Surathkal to Mangalore and part of NH-48 upto B.C Road
and is nearing completion. The stretch between Kundapur to Surathkal and Mangalore (19 km.) to
Kerala Border (Talpadi) (16 km.) has started and is expected to be completed in three years. The

condition and road was closed intermittently during last three years for strengthening of road. At

major state roads in the D.K. District.

between Karkala to Shringeri falls in the Ghat section. Therefore, heavy vehicles from Hospet-
Bellary region to the port do not use this route.

36

NH-48 connecting New Mangalore Port under the “Port Connectivity Programme” of the National
Highway Development Programme (NHDP). The work of 4-laning of NH-17 from Surathkal to

prove inadequate to handle the future traffic that will flow through the primary and secondary
hinterland of the region.
Murmugao Port
199. The Committee was informed that road connectivity in the Mormugao Port is through
NH-4A and NH-17. The single lane road is making traffic movement very slow and current traffic
congestions. The 4-lane road connecting to NH-17 is incomplete and bulk cargo traffic like coal
and met coal is adversely affected. A 4-lane road connecting the Bangalore-Mumbai will ease the
traffic. The highway from Verna to Mormugao Harbour work is stalled at Mangor and a balance
of 5.2 km. is yet to be completed due to objections of the State Government. This road may also
benefit the new additional berth of 270 meters which is to be completed by 2011. The coal laden
vehicles are polluting the town at present.
200. The Committee was also informed that additional berth of 450 meters is under construction
at the Murmugao Port while the road connecting the berth is not sufficient to bear the traffic
generated by the time. This road which connect the Harbour has to be completed simultaneously
so that the benefit of extra handling may be better utilized as the modernization projects are to be
completed by 2012.
Paradip Port
201. The port of Paradip is basically a service provider to the traders and suppliers and the main
economic activities of the Port is earning of foreign exchange through export/import of cargoes like
Coal, Iron Ore, Charge chrome, Ferro Chrome, Chrome Ore and other ores, fertilizer and sugar
etc. A Good transport network is a vital requirement for steady supply of Cargoes in accordance
with the demand of the trader. NH-5A connects Paradip to various important roads the country.
The roads from Cuttack to Paradip has vital role in the ever growth of Paradip Port.
202. The Committee has observed that road congestion is a regular feature at the NH-5A because
of over crowding of trucks on both the ways. 1t was learnt that over 3000 loaded trucks are
coming and going to the Paradip Port on a daily basis. The Committee was informed that the sorry
state of the NH-5A started since the super cyclone in the year 1999. However, the little bit of
efforts made for the road development is lagging behind of schedule and about 50% of thus 90
km. road is still under various stages of construction causing difficulties to the general public, huge
losses of resources such as fuel, time and even causes very dear to innocent lives of people at
the time of emergency medical assistance. However, the information provided by the NHAI states
that only the rehabilitation of old Mahanadi bridge at 67
th km. is only pending. The Committee
noticed that the work of NH 5A was started on February 2004 with a total estimated cost of
Rs.327.77 crores. The project was to be completed after 3 years. However, the works are yet to
be over even a lapse of nearly 7 years.
Visakhapatnam Port
203. The Committee was informed that Visakhapatnam Port has formed a Joint Venture with
NHAI to execute the projects of road connectivity and 12 km. road connecting the Port to National
Highway has been commissioned. Improvement of 2-lane roads to 4-lane roads and construction
of flyovers/ramps etc. will be taken-up in co-ordination with NHAI.

37
Cochin Port
204. The hinterland connection of the Cochin Port is through the Ernakulam city. The Wellingdon
Island, where Cochin Port is situated was then connected to the mainland of Ernakulam though a

tremendously. This will further increase in future. Though one more bridge connecting, Wellingdon

congested city areas is causing severe 1ocal and social problems. As such possibility of providing

proposed, has to be vigorously followed up for early implementation. In the absence of flyovers

posing a serious problem in the city areas. Since the ICTT Vallarpadam proposed to handle 2.5
million TEUs per year, the movement of container trucks will excessively increase. The
Committee recommends that in order to ease the road congestion, National Waterway
passing through hinterland of Cochin Port may be developed.
Kolkata Port
205. Kolkata Port is well connected with National and State highways, railways and national
waterways, KDS is connected with NH-6, NH-2 and NH-34 through city roads. NH-41 connects
HDC with NH-6 and rest of the country.
Tuticorin Port
206. The proposed dedicated freight corridor linking Tuticorin-Erode-Nagpur for the easy
movement of cargo from the central parts of the country to the port may be expedited. The
Committee hopes that the projects of 4-laning of NH 7A (47.2 km.) to Tirunelveli and NH 45B
(128.5 km.) to Madurai which are the major road connectivity to the Port will be completed as
per their scheduled completion date. The Committee also recommends that construction of
Turicorin-Kollam Express way may be materialized for the ease of road connectivity to the
Port.

Road Company Ltd. along with NHAI, Government of Tamil Nadu and Ennore Port Ltd. for
upgrading the Northern corridor from the Port to the National Highway system. The project
estimated to cost Rs.600 crores for improving the connecting roads viz. Fishing Harbour Road
from the northern gate, Ennore expressway, Manali Oil Refinery road, TPP Road and northern
segment of the inner ring roads for a total length of 30 km. Shore protection measures along the
Ennore Coast have been completed and substantial portion of project affecting families have been
moved to the housing units specially constructed for them north of Ennore Expressway. The
project is likely to be completed by end of 2013.
208. In order to upgrade the access to the Southern/Western corridor from the Port to the
National Highway, an elevated port link road to Maduravoyal for a length of 19 km. has been
planned partially along the Cooum river bank and over the NH-4.  This project was awarded to a

cargo evacuation from the Port without congesting the intervening city roads.
209. The Ministry in their reply has informed the status of various road projects of Port’s
connectivity. In Chennai-Ennore Port three contracts of road projects has been terminated for

38
which the work commenced in May 2006-07. As such no work has taken place. In. Murmagao
port connectivity on NH 17 B the work is to be completed in Oct., 2011 and 6% of the work
has progressed. The work is delayed due to encroachment.
210. The Committee observes that most of the projects of road connectivity have delayed
due to one or the other reasons and most of the roads maintained by Government
department are in bad shape and the maintenance more often are behind the schedule. This
shows the casual attitude of the Ministry towards the Major Ports.
211. The Committee observes that road connectivity is not adequate to cater to the needs
of the existing traffic in the Ports. Road widening and upgrading process are not up to the
requirement of the current day development needs of the Port. The Committee recommends
that road widening and other interlinking plans as proposed by the Ports need to be taken
with the Ministry of RTH at the highest levels for its speedy completion. The Committee
also recommends that the addition of infrastructure in the recent time should be taken into
consideration while formulating the road connectivity upgradation projects to the Port.
212. The Committee observes that port connectivity to NMPT is insufficient as the
connectivity to National Highways is poor, heavily congested and not suitable for heavy
truck traffic. The Committee recommends that Government should accede to Port’s request
for the NHAI to take up improvement to the NH-48 and NH-13 under Port Connectivity
(PC) programme of the National Highway Development Programme (NHDP) so that the ban
on passage or heavy vehicles could be lifted on these stretches. The Committee recommends
for widening and strengthening of Chitradurga-Mangalore stretch of NH-13 so that the
distance between Hospet-Bellary region and the port will be reduced by 150 km.
213. The Committee is of the view that at least 4-lane road connectivity is required in all
the Ports. Uniform infrastructure facilities may be made in all the Major Ports so that the
goals and bench marking of port operations may be attained and performance monitoring
also may be possible. At present there is transportation problem inside the port for cargo
movement from eastern side gate to the western side gate of the Visakhapatnam port and
vice versa . Necessary flyovers and roads will be able to solve the problem. Evacuation of
cargo from the port and movement to the port areas need to be properly synchronized so
that inter-modal network functions smoothly.
214. Poor maintenance of roads in India leads to accidents and also forces vehicles to
move at a slow pace, resulting in loss of time and energy. There has not been much
development of road and rail infrastructure which can meet the requirement of Major Ports.
One reason is multiple agencies at the centre such as Ministry of Road Transport and
Highways, Ministry of Railways and Ministry of Shipping and the lack of coordination among
them. The Committee recommends that there should be a coordinating agency to oversee
the rail and road connectivity at the Ports. The Committee recommends that the local self
governments such as municipal entities also made the stakeholders in the development
process.
215. The Committee is of the opinion that a good road and rail connectivity will enhance
any port’s business potential and in the case of Ennore Port, its development and rail and
road connectivity have not progressed in tandem. The Committee feels that Ennore Port has
abundant virgin land to create world class facility, however, the Port is not in a position to
reach its peak in the absence of proper planning at the early stage of conceptualization of
the Port for good connectivity using all modes of transport. The Committee feels that
critical rail connectivity from Athipattu to Ennore and the new line between Puttur and
Athipattu which will provide a shorter route for iron-ore traffic to Ennore Port should be

39
expedited at the earliest. The Committee also feels that the approach roads to the Port from
National Highways should be widened so that movement of heavy vehicles carrying cargo to
Port is not hindered.
IT, Security and Traffic Monitoring
216. The Committee was informed that all the Major Ports are manned by CISF. All the Ports
have access control CCTVs for the security of the port. Two high speed patrol boats are engaged
for patrolling the port waters. Vessel Traffic Management System (VTMS)/Radar/Automatic
Identification System (AIS) are used to identify all the vessels within the port waters. Joint Coastal
patrolling is conducted by Local Police, Customs and CISF to patrol the sea side upto 5 nautical
miles upto the shore. Beyond 5 nautical miles it is the combined responsibility of coast Guard and
Navy. Maritime States have also set up Coastal Police Station along the coast and some police
stations are either close to the port area or within the port premises.
217. Coast Guard and Navy are represented among the trustees notified by the Ministry of
Shipping to enable the management to keep regular liaison with these security agencies. Regular
meetings are being held at port level and in the State Secretariat involving all the security/law
enforcement agencies like Police, Navy, Coast Guard, Customs, IB etc.
218. All the Major Ports are International Ships and Port Security Code (ISPS) compliant,
according to the International Maritime Organization (IMO) Code. The security audits of all the
Major Ports are regularly conducted by DG (Shipping). IB has also conducted separate security
drills and suggested methods for improvement periodically.
219. V essel Traffic Management System (VTMS) is a real-time software that helps port operators
manage the vessels in port waters. VTMS system at Mumbai Port was installed for safe navigation
and surveillance in May, 1997 which has already outlived its life and accordingly Global Tender was
invited in October, 2008 for replacement with latest state of the art technology VTMS. For the
scheme an estimate amounting Rs.36.41 crores has been sanctioned by the Board on 31.03.2008.
220. Mumbai Port has hosted its own website viz. http://www.mumbaiport.gov.in which provides
details regarding tariff rates, weather conditions, tender notice and auction sale notice, port
performance, port layout and latest development. About 300 VHF sets comprising Base/Mobile and
Walkie Talkie sets are in use at various departments like Marine, Security, Mechanical Engineering,
Civil Defence, Port Fire and Safety etc. Further, Solar Power Generation System is installed on
Flotilla and Light Houses for operational use of VHF sets.
221. The Committee was informed that the New Mangalore Port has taken up LAN work for
total computerization of the Port which would emphasize e-business suiting to computerization in
day to day activities of the Port operations and in all other departments. It also enables to
synchronize the operations/transactions linking with the PCS/Indian Customs Electronic
Data Interchange Systems. The work is under progress and is expected to be completed by
November, 2010.
222. The New Mangalore Port has undertaken the Security Surveillance and monitoring system
of the activities within the Port and installed CCTV as per the requirement of ISPS. Speed boat
has been put into operation for patrolling by the CISF in the port waters. Bio metric attendance
system already implemented for booking the cargo handling workers. RFID attendance system for
the entire staff is under implementation. In order to maintain the sustainable development of the
Port, it has taken up many projects for keeping the port area and surroundings green and clean.
Being an ISO 9001:2008 certified Port, NMPT is in the process of obtaining ISO 14001-2004
certification.

40
223. The VTMS will enable the New Mangalore Port to ensure navigational safety in the vessel
traffic movement in the harbour and detect the movements any unauthorized or unscheduled vessels
in the area. The operation of the system will help to prevent accidental collision/grounding/damages
etc. VTMS also covers the security of Port-Based Special Economic Zones at V allarpadam and at
Puthuvypeen of the Cochin Port where vital installations such as single point mooring facility
(SPM) and the storage tank farm of BPCL-KRL situated. VTMS installation in the Cochin Port is
a major step towards ensuring security and safety of the entire coastal waters around the port
limits of Cochin Port Trust.
224. The Committee was informed that computerization project covers computerization of all
areas of Cochin Port Trust including the processes related to port users and internal back office
processes to improve its all-round efficiency, transparency and objectivity leading to good
governance. Cochin Port has selected the best of breed products and vendors including ERP from
SAP, GIS from ESRI and Port Operations for implementing the above project. The project also
covers the integration with the Port Community System being implemented by the Indian Port
Association. Cochin Port is the first port in India that has gone in for Computerisation of all its
activities from end to end integrating an ERP solution with the port operations and GIS software.
225. The Computerisation at Kolkata Port is to ensure improved customer-focus leading to
minimized transaction costs and efficient port operations with eventual paperless transactions, a
comprehensive Information Technology (IT) infrastructure is in advanced stage of completion. The
system includes Port Community System, Port Operation and Management System, Executive
Information System, Facilities Access Management, etc.
226. The Committee is of the view that in the present context and given the fact that
India has vast coast line extending to 7517 km., Port security is to be given utmost
importance for the security of the nation and smooth trade. The Committee notes that all
the Major Ports are ISPS compliant. But that fact should not bring complacency in the
efforts and more is need for constant vigil in port and sea area. The Committee observes
that there is lack of coordination in various agencies involved in security of Mumbai Port.
The Committee, recommend that the Ministry of Shipping should take up the matter with
the concerned of Centre and State Government agencies and evolve a permanent
Mechanism to address the problems.
227. The computerization and web-based operations are the need of the hour. Due to lack
of sufficient IT implementation the Major Ports are still facing multiple problems in terms
of voluminous documentation, inconsistency in data, duplication of work, redundant book
keepings, these problems have led to lower productivity and non working time at berths.
The Vessel Traffic Management System (VTMS) facilities are used for regular berthing/
deberthing of ships. The Committee observes that only Mumbai Port is having VTMS
facilities and the VTMS projects are under implementation at Kandla, Kochi and
Vallarpadam Ports. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that majority of the
Major Ports are not equipped with VTMS facilities which has affected their efficiency. The
Committee recommends that IT infrastructure should be installed for exchange of
Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) messages between Major Ports and other stakeholders.
The Committee also recommends that all Major Ports should undertake an assessment of
utility of documents involved in various operations and web enabled services should be made
available to port users. The Committee recommends that proper training facilities for
handling the modern monitoring systems need to he provided to the concerned personnel
operating such equipments.
228. The Committee observes that Port Security is having utmost importance and all the
concerned departments may be kept on vigil in this matter. The Committee is of the view

41
that extended use of IT will supplement its effort of making in port and sea area safe and
secure by tracking movement of suspected dangerous vessels.  The Committee came to know
about the threats of various kinds to the Port personnel and property as also interference
in their day-to-day functioning at port from local mafias/goons. The Committee takes
serious view of the development and recommends that adequate security may be provided
to port officials so that they can discharge their functions/duties without fear and
interference.
Land Policy/Problems
229. The Ministry informed that keeping in view the critical role played by Ports and to sustain
and improve the efficiency it was felt to review the extant policies and suggest mid-term
corrections, wherever necessary, in various policies governing the Major Ports. The review
committee set up in 2009 observed that land policy is one of the significant policy frameworks
guiding the overall functioning of port sector. Ports land has been used for carrying out economic
activity such as establishing industry to ensure captive cargo to the port and allotting land for
setting up SEZ for developing industrial development in and around Ports. Optimum utilization of
land is important. The review committee devised a policy to be followed by the Ports which
includes fresh allotment, lease, general etc. and is effective from 13
th January, 2011. Prior to this,
land Policy-2004 in Major Port was effective and all the decisions to lease out port lands were
given/taken based on the guidelines given therein.
230. The Committee was informed that Paradip Port was readier started as a State Government
project and was later on transferred to Government of India in the year 1965. As per the
agreement, all the movable and immovable assets belonged to the project would be taken over by
the Central Government. However, the formalities of regularization of the revenue records in favour
of Paradip Port Trust for 6382.07 acres are yet to be done.
231. The Committee was informed that Ennore Port has requested the Salt Department of
Government of Tamil Nadu to transfer 1164.5567 acres for its developmental activities. The request
of Ennore Port for such a transfer was made in August, 2001. Taking into consideration the price
paid by TIDCO to Salt Department for acquiring salt land at the price of Rs.35,000/- per acre in
2003, Ennore Port made an offer of Rs.50,000/- per acre in 2004. Of late, Salt Department has
come out with a proposal to consider the transaction/market value of land in that area for fixing
price of its land. Such transaction/market value is guided by different factors like making long term
investment, in real estate, etc. Because of this, the valuation of Salt Department land has gone up
unreasonably and the rate of escalation in the value of land has also become unpredictable. Around
2 years back, Salt Department has transferred land to NTPC and HPCL at the rate of Rs.9,00,000/-
per acre and Rs.18,00,000/- per acre respectively. In May 2010, Salt Department has transferred
35 acres of land to Ennore Port at the provisional cost of Rs.36,69,418/- per acre.
232. The Committee observed that the land transferring issue is a hindrance to various
Port expansion projects of the Paradip Port. The Committee therefore recommends that all
the disputes may be settled amicably and the transfer of land may be done at the earliest
so that it may speed up the modernization projects at Paradip.
233. The Mumbai Port’s 753 hectares land is contiguous with the land of the city of
Mumbai and has become an integral part of the city. Real Estate is one of the key assets
of Mumbai Port and care has to be taken to ensure that its land usage policy is carefully
monitored in the future. The Committee is aware that the demand for land is aggravating
in most of the cities and Mumbai is not the only one. The expansion of the city limits is
now a problem with the port and vested interests are making all out efforts for grabbing
the land of the port. The Committee therefore recommends that a clear-cut land policy may

42
be made for proper utilization of the land with the Port. The Committee also recommends
that every effort should be made to protect the land of the port from encroachment.
234. The Committee was informed by the stakeholder that the Mumbai port is earning
exorbitant rental on land leases to the operators. The recent tariff revisions were made on
retrospective effect which reportedly causing financial liability to the land users. The
Committee is of the view that the Port authorities may discuss the matter with port users
and review the order taking in view the commercial viability of activities.
235. The Committee is of the view that land price issue as regards the Ennore Port may
be settled amicably with the State Government.
Environment
236. The Committee was informed that existing/proposed CRZ notifications for implementation,
imposes certain restrictions on the developmental activities at the port which are to be taken up
essentially along the coastal areas. In most of the Ports where land area is scarce and optimum
utilization of the available area will not be possible due to the imposed restrictions. The areas
available with the Port are earmarked for meeting the requirements of its future expansion/
modernization. The application of CRZ norms affect the entire programme of expansion/
modernization. Hence, there is need to have special status for the existing Major Ports so as to
accommodate their planned expansion.
237. CRZ clearance for three PPP projects like 2
nd coal terminal at berth no.7 iron ore terminal
west of breakwater and coal terminal at berth no. 11 are pending. It was informed that public
hearing which is mandatory by the State authorities is not yet organized and hence there is delay.
238. The sea shore/backwaters are just on the door step in most of the places in and around
the Cochin Port area and as such insisting on the standard conditions would completely hamper
the Port development. Though it has a very strategic location being close to the trunk trade routes,
land scarcity in Willington Island constrains its development proposals. As such Port proposes to
go in for expansion through outer harbour projects for which development works on the V ypeen
coast areas would be required to be taken up, which would however be difficult, if the standard
conditions are to be adhered to. Hence it was submitted that by developing reclamation wall around
the sea shores and by imposing certain environment management conditions like development of
sewage treatment plant, day to day monitoring of environment conditions and banning sewage or
any other debris into the sea, permission should be granted to develop port related facilities near
the shore.
239. The Committee was informed that the following steps are taken to minimize pollution
emanating from Iron ore and coal at various Ports:
* sprinkling of water on cargo, roads and storage plots
* installation of wind barriers
* covering trucks with tarpaulin sheet to prevent dust
* cleaning of truck tyres before allowing them into the city
* Plantation of trees within the ports.
240. The Committee is of the view that port operations can be made environment friendly
by developing reclamation wall around the sea snores and by imposing certain environment
management conditions like development of sewage treatment plant, day to day monitoring
of environment conditions and banning sewage or any other debris into the sea. Otherwise,

43
the Committee is afraid that if the Ports are not allowed to carry out its developmental
activities given the environmental regulations the Ports’ efficiency would be substantially
affected and may lead to under-utilisation of resources at the port. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the matter may be taken up with the Ministry of Environment
and Forest to consider the proposal of Major Ports and may be allowed to execute their
developmental projects.
241. The Committee notes that environmental pollution caused by trafficking of bulk
cargos like iron ore, coal, sulphur, rock phosphate, crude oil, gas, fertilizers, chemicals, etc.
are very frequent in the Port areas. The sprinkling of water is carried out on dusty cargo
but the problem of pollution has not been addressed satisfactorily. The Committee is of the
view that laxity in taking adequate steps to check the pollution cast by port operations can
prove to be expensive. The Committee would like to invite the attention of the Government
to the media reports stating that Madras High Court has ordered Chennai Port Trust to
move coal and iron ore out of Chennai Port to the Ennore Port.  This move is likely to
cause a loss of revenue amounting to Rs.250 crores annually and render 5000 workers
jobless. It is also reported that stopping coal and iron ore handling by the Chennai Port may
also affect supply to electricity generating units and cement plans in Tamil Nadu. The
Committee is afraid that unilateral decision to shift these cargoes to Ennore may prove
counter productive and benefit the private Ports as the stakeholders have other options and
may move to private Ports. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government
should come forward to help the Chennai Port to sort out the problems. The Committee
hopes that the Government will take care of the interest of the 5000 employees likely to
be affected by shifting the cargoes to Ennore Port and ensure that there will be no
retrenchment as directed by the Hon’ble Court.
242. The Committee also recommends that Government should direct the Major Ports to
explore modern ways of cargo handling and storage in order to reduce the environmental
pollutions. The Committee is of the view that keeping a pollution free environment is a
social obligation, therefore, Government may also consider funding the cost of pollution
checking operations by the Ports.
243. At present, environment clearance is to be obtained separately for each individual
port project, which causes a lot of delay in the project implementation. The Committee is
of the view that the issues related with the Ministries of Commerce, Environment & Forest,
etc. need to be discussed at the Ministry level so that a common policy for all the Ports
could be formulated. Since the Environment and Forest Ministry is considering the
individual cases separately because of the complex nature of the geographical distribution
of the country, the cases could be taken up by the Ministry of Shipping for pursuing the
matter. The Committee, therefore, recommends that within the port limits, Ports may be
permitted to prepare Coastal Zone Management Plan (CZMP), taking into consideration the
future construction/expansion requirements and also commitments if any, based on earlier
environment clearances issued. The proposed new environment guidelines/norms, which are
not in line with the earlier commitments should not be made applicable in case of existing
ports and the norms should be in such a way that they do not hamper the future
development. Only in cases where Ports can spare green area shall such norms be insisted
upon; i.e., relaxations, exemptions of the guidelines/norms, on a case to case basis shall be
permissible.
244. The Committee also recommends that efforts should be made to set up green Ports-
by installing wind and solar power centres, with CNG fitted vehicles, water harvesting and
forestation. Enhancing the port capacity in a sustainable way, better water and waste

44
management, reduction of emissions from fuels, switching over to non-conventional energy
sources etc, should be taken up to save the environment.
Storage Space for Cargo
245. Considering the constraints of expansion of existing Ports, the site in the vicinity of the
Ports are developed to supplement the storage capacity to boost industrial activity to ensure cargo
growth.
246. Mumbai Port has approximately 7 lakh square meters of open and covered storage
accommodation for storing un-cleared, confiscated goods  and hazardous cargo. Iron and steel
constitutes the highest share of traffic at the docks both for export and import. The key exporters
are mainly the steel plants in and around Mumbai/Maharashtra. These entities perceive Mumbai port
as their natural choice of a port, given its proximity. There is a substantial amount of traffic for
the scrap, machinery, and project cargo as well. The machinery and project cargo generally require
more storage space. Some subcategories, like galvanized steel, require closed storage space.
247. The Port considers motor vehicles as strategic commodity, acknowledges that it is a space
eater. For the imports, delayed evacuation by the importers and the custom clearance in the case
of private vehicles are the main issues that the port faces today.
248. Sugar supply is seasonal and there is very little activity during the monsoon season. The
movement to the part is almost entirely by rail. Sugar comes in bags and a large number of
workers are required for handling and stacking. Sugar requires closed storage.
249. The Committee found that the iron ore, fertilizer raw materials, etc. were lying open at the
Port premises. The improper way of its storage is a matter of great concern as it affects the
quality of the materials to a great extent as a result huge revenue lass may be happened. Moreover,
the windy atmosphere is carrying away a portion of the iron ore dust with it which ultimately
results in the environmental pollution in the area.
250. The Committee was informed that the Visakhapatnam Port is facing space constraint in
finding proper stocking area. Land acquisition is the major problem especially because of the
closeness of the port to the city limits. The Committee was informed that an alternative option to
overcome the limitation with the port is to acquire 42 acres of land on the outskirts far which the
approval of the Ministry of Shipping is awaited.
251. Even though, there are covered storage space it is not maintained wel1 adequate state of
the art covered warehousing facility may be erected at the Parts so as to increase traffic and to
ensure job opportunities of the Port workers.
252. The Ministry informed that instructions have been issued to dispose off the unclaimed and
abandoned goods in the manner specified under section 62 of Major Parts Act, 1963. Major Part
Trust Act, 1963 provides, far disposal of unclaimed and abandoned goods after 60 days of arrival
in the port and considering the perishable and dangerous in nature, the goods can be disposed even
without waiting for the 60 days time limit.
253. All the dangerous and highly inflammable goods are to be stored and handled by observing
safe handling practices as per IMD all the Major Parts are handling all verities of cargo including
hazardous and dang emus in nature. Customs Department verify the permissibility of impart and
export by enforcing EXIM policy declared by the Commerce Ministry. The Major Ports are only
facilitating safe transport storage and handling of the cargo. All the Major Ports have regulations
notified as per IDMG code of International Maritime Organization laying down the manner of
handling storage and transportation of dangerous and hazardous goods.

45
254. During the visit of the Committee to various Major Parts, some of the stakeholders pointed
out that imparted food items/grains are not evacuated from the part far want of lab test reports/
certificate which are received after mare than two weeks. When the matter was brought to the
notice of Ministry of Shipping, they submitted that the food items/grains imparted are required to
be tested in the food testing laboratory before they are cleared out of the port. However, many
of the Parts are lacking such facilities in the adjoining areas. As a result of which the food samples
are get tested at a distant location which causes undue delay in the disposal of the food items. In
certain cases such delay causes decay of the food items whereby all the efforts became a futile
act. The Ministry of Shipping has taken up this difficulty with the Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare.
255. The Committee notes that thousands of acres of land is in possession of Major Ports
and they are more know as ‘landlord Ports’. The Committee is however constrained to note
that Major Ports are facing acute shortage of storage space which has affected cargo
aggregation/evacuation. It also affects the discharge/loading of vessels. The Committee
recommends that proper storage facility may be planned in such a manner depending on the
type of cargo handled by the Port. Similarly such storage places could be equipped with
direct cargo transfer conveyor belts so that the double handling of the same cargo could be
avoided. The Committee recommends that additional space can also be created by
demolishing redundant structures and that the un-cleared goods, warehouse activities which
include unaccompanied baggage clearing etc. should be shifted to outer areas.
256. The Committee had observed at Paradip Port that iron ore and coal are accumulated
open around the port premises. The Committee therefore recommends that the waste
disposal mechanism should be made operational in all the Ports in order to avoid
accumulation of huge dumping yards around the port premises.
257. The Committee notes that environmental clearance norms are cumbersome and
causes undue delays due to which the projects get delayed. The Committee recommends that
separate lands may be earmarked for specific types of cargo so that basic facilities to handle
such specific cargo could be developed. The usage formula should be confined to the specific
purpose only so that wastage of resources could be checked.
258. The Committee notes that inspection/testing facilities for imported food items/grains
are highly inadequate at the Major Ports and getting the reports/certificates from the
specialized laboratories located at a distant place takes more that two weeks time. The
Committee therefore recommends that adequate number of food testing laboratories may be
established in the premises of Major Ports for speedy disposal of perishable food articles.
The Committee also recommends that till the testing facilities are set up at the Ports,
Government may consider the possibility to allow test reports/certificates issued by the
accredited testing laboratories. Since the food import is an unavoidable phenomenon
therefore even at a short notice matter is to be taken up with utmost care and seriousness.
The Committee further recommends that adequate number of Drug Controlling Officers
may be deputed near the port vicinity to avoid delay in cargo clearance.
Wage Policy/Contractual Labour Issues
259. The efficiency of any organization depends upon the productivity of its workforce. The
Committee was informed that manpower has been reduced considerably from the initial strength
including officers and dock workers in the New Mangalore Port. There is no direct recruitment
to the Ports since long. It was also informed that many of the staff has attained the age of
superannuation and the Port is not moving for recruitments instead they are out sourcing services.
The Visakhapatnam Port employee unions have alleged that leakage of administrative and security

46
information is being benefited by the private agencies. The good employee-employer relation does
not exist. The quality of work and response to the needy hours are lacking. The management is
now vulnerable to malpractices, prompt response are lacking at the administration level. The  lack
of proper training to the staff is evident at every aspect of their method of working. Staff selection
is not done as per the job requirement.
260. The Committee was informed that approximately 1500 vacancies as per schedule of
employees of Cochin Part are lying vacant as on date. Due to this the entry level works are
suffered very badly.
261. The representatives of employees’ unions of Visakhapatnam Port complained that
privatization of the major activities of  the Visakhapatnam Port by means of outsourcing etc. are
adversely affecting the working culture of employees as well as the profit making of the Port.
Many works like development of WQ6, EQ10, mechanized coal handling facility, mechanized
unloading facility, development of docks, extension of the existing container terminal, crane
services etc. have already come under private operators. The back bone of the Visakhapatnam Port
is iron ore handling unit which is also under active consideration for private participation. Such
activities are adversely affecting the future or about 800 employees of the Visakhapatnam Part Trust.
262. The Committee was informed that the contract workers are not getting minimum wages
even though Government is making payment for  this. Middlemen are milking from  the situation.
Also there is no job guarantee and other facilities like health, EPF and other welfare activities are
applicable to them.
263. The Committee was also informed that NSICT and GTI terminals of Jawharlal Nehru Part
are paying the workers less than the minimum wages and denied coverage under the mandatory
EPF Act. The JNPT is a mute spectator to these and no effective measures so far has been taken
apart from issuing periodic circulars. The strict enforcement of the labour law is not there at
JNPT. Transport workers are deployed for  12-14 hours duty without rest intervals. There are no
scheduled shift timings for the workers at the Jawharlal Nehru Part.
264. The Committee was informed that engagement of contract workers in Paradip Part for the
muck cleaning spillage removal work and railway maintenance work are making discontentment
among the workers. Even though Paradip Part has manpower to handle the work, outsourcing of
manpower is done at coal handling plant, iron are handling plant, hospitals, schools etc. which
results in no work for  the regular employees.
265. The  Committee was also informed that car drivers (around 100) are working an contract
basis for  the Paradip Port Trust.  They are not provided with identity cards, uniforms etc. More
than 750 temporary workers are not getting EPF and ESI benefits even though they are working
since the last 15 to 20 years. Regularization of their jab was demanded by the employee unions.
Minimum wages are not ensured to them. However, the Paradip Part management had informed
that the minimum wage norm is ensured by them as per their contract terms and conditions.
266. Till 1998, Compassionate appointment at Tuticorin Port has been made without any
reference to ceiling limit. 71 legal heirs were waiting since 1993 onwards for  seeking appointments
on compassionate grounds. 5% ceiling limit in filling up of post under compassionate appointment,
this port is unable to fill up the post in addition to the panel for three years also affected the
beneficiaries since their name could not be included in the panel for compassionate appointment.
It is, therefore, necessary to relax the ceiling limit and on one time relaxation of the ceiling for
some years.
267. Fixation of basic pay as per new revised scale caused a lot of anomaly among the seniors
and juniors due to wrong interpretation in fixing the basic pay. 3% increment has only been allowed

47
in the certain cadres. Merger of Tuticorin Port Trust Cargo Handling Labour Pool Workers with
the Port strength is another long pending demand. It was also alleged that in Tuticorin Port Trust,
despite repeated efforts the Port Management has been adamant in regularizing the canteen
employees as Port Employees. Due to ban on recruitment, there is a shortage of skilled man power
which is a major bottleneck for development of the port.
268. The Committee was informed that Mumbai Port has its own medical facilities and operates
them with the help of its own employees. A modem hospital complex well equipped with latest
sophisticated gadgets has been provided at Wadala for its employees. The Committee was informed
that the doctors and the paramedical staff are engaged on contract basis.
269. The Committee notes that there has been tendency now a day to engage workmen
on contract basis in Government owned PSUs. The Committee is dismay to note that
workmen even after service of 10-20 years are not regularized and they are denied of other
benefits also. The Committee also received complaints of under payment to workers in
violation of Minimum Wages Act. The Committee recommends that PSU should not shy
away from meeting their social obligation. The Government should ensure that workers who
had served for many decades must be considered for regularization. The Committee
recommends that regular appointments may be made to fill the vacant posts so that the
hospital may become more service oriented. The Committee also recommends that the
compassionate appointment should be restored without any conditions. Since regular trained
workforce is required for the Port’s functioning, the in-house as well as outdoor training
facilities may be explored along with the modernization projects.
270. The Committee was informed that the Indian Maritime University has the modern facilities
to impart training to the officers and employees of the Ports. Also there is provision to get training
abroad on maritime and Ports operations. The Committee has the view that different Ports may
be handling different type of equipments and machineries as per the type of cargo handled
in each case. Therefore, the training requirement also may be port specific especially at
certain technical fields. It is better to adopt a training strategy not for academic purposes
but for the practical utility so that a trained person would be able to handle all the
operational know-how of a particular area. Such a pool of trained manpower is required for
each port immediately before modern equipment is installed there. A long term training
plan may be formulated with the sole aim that the productivity per staff is maintained in
the upward track.
271. The Committee also received complaints that SC/ST employees are deprived of getting
important/key positions in the port administration wing and they have to face harassment from the
top Management of Visakhapatnam Port Trust and special training for SC/ST employees to suit for
feeder grade promotion is not provided. Promotions of eligible feeder grade SC/ST officers to the
post of Assistant Secretary/Accounts Officer is not done in Paradip Port Trust.
272. The Committee is of the view that certain issues as mentioned by the employees are
needed to be looked into an unbiased manner. The sectarian approach should not be
tolerated and immediate intervention should be required. In the case of posts require
specific training and qualifications, those employees who may be in the zone of
consideration of such posts may be provided with adequate training if necessary so that such
avenues could be made accessible to the persons from SC/ST categories.
273. The Committee was informed in the meetings with the Port workers representatives that
private agencies are operating in the Mormugao Port especially in areas which are strategically
sensitive. The Committee was also informed that only 30% of the workers are from the Port side
and all the others have been hired from private agencies.

in consultation with the local bodies.

to a suitable location is also required for further development of the Port. There is no concrete
progress made in the matter despite many rounds of talks with the authorities. Proper rehabilitation
of the affected people may be made.

benefit the cruise vessels. The road development has importance in the tourism
development as well.

control of the Paradip Port Trust. There are large numbers of population inhabiting that area and

situated at plot no.1, Brundaban Colony, Paradip is struggling for proper infrastructure and financial
aid from the municipal and port authorities. Because of this other developmental activities are at
a stand still. The Committee notes that a large population directly and indirectly related to
Paradip Port are without benefits of Port activities. This situation has created discontent
among the local people and may cause serious problem for the Port. The Committee is of
the opinion that this is a serious issue which needs to be taken up with the State

matter of Sitaram Sarswat U P School in consultation with the State authorities to solve the

adopted. The Committee also recommends that training of the staff to modern equipments

system on the part of the port management.

Autonomy in Major Ports
289. The Committee was informed that the Ports enjoy adequate autonomy in as much as the
delegated financial powers to the Ports are exercised by Board/HoD. The extent of autonomy to
the Port is reviewed from time-to-time depending upon their experience and needs.
290. The Port Trusts are autonomous bodies functioning under the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963.
The powers that are delegated to Ports for undertaking various works, taking loan, sanction of
projects etc. are reviewed from time to time. As far as private ports are concerned, they are under
the administrative control of respective Maritime States and not covered under the MPT Act, 1963.
These private Ports or non-Major Ports are getting more cargo share of the total cargo handled
in India mainly because they are new, have large investment and infrastructure equipped with latest
technology. The Ministry of Shipping is in the process of giving more autonomy to the Major Ports
by way of corporatization. Already Ennore Port Ltd., which is a major port, has been corporatized,
Ministry of Shipping is in the process of corporatizing more Ports in the line of EPL pursuant to
a meeting taken by Hon’ble Prime. Minister on 3
rd February, 2010. After corporatization, the Major
Ports would be in a position to have more financial power as per the delegation of powers
applicable to the PSUs. At present EPL, which also enjoy mini-ratna status can take investment
decision upto Rs.500 crores. Further, the Ministry informed that the delegation of financial power
is an ongoing process and orders are issued from time to time.
291. The Committee was informed that the existing administrative, financial and other powers
with the Major Ports are not proving to be bottleneck to the developmental activities of the Ports.
The Major Ports have been given administrative and financial powers for entering into contracts
for plan and non-plan, for maintenance dredging, to raise over draft and power to charge
expenditure to capital. As far as developmental work is concerned, the Port Trust Board has been
delegated power of Rs.50 crores for new projects and Rs.100 crores for replacement as per Annual
Plan approved by the Government subject to the delegation of powers from time to time.
292. The enactment of the Major Port Trusts Act in 1963 marked a new milestone in the
evolution of the port laws in India in relation to Act of 1908. The Major Port Trusts Act, 1963

51
for the first time laid out the institutional framework for creation of a separate port authorities for
each major port and defined the powers and functions of such a port authority in respect of all
aspects of port functioning. Until enactment of Major Port Trusts Act, 1963, the major and minor
Ports in India were directly under the administrative control of the Central or State Government
and were managed through a separate ministry or a departmental organization. It was also informed
that the Major Ports are functioning under the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963 and the powers that
are delegated to Ports are reviewed from time to time. However, the Committee has been informed
by all the Ports. about the delay in decision making by the government on most of their
administrative and modernization programmes as a result by which the major works are get delayed
at various levels of implementation. It is true that the delay is causing very dearer to the Major
Ports whereby the adjoining private Ports are benefiting out of the situation.
293. A major amendment to Major Port Trust Act of 1963 was notified in 1997, following the
announcement of Guidelines on Participation of Private Sector in Indian Port Sector in 1996. The
amendment brought into being Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP), to independently regulate
the fixation of various port related tariffs, to be charged by Major Ports. The TAMP sought to
ensure a level playing field between the upcoming private port developers entering the Indian port
sector and the existing Major Ports.
294. The passage of the Act also paved the way for decentralization and rationalization of port
administration. Despite its salutary effects, the MPT Act, 1963 has lately been criticized for its
limiting provisions in the post-liberalisation phase in the development of Indian port sector.
295. In response to a question as to the criteria to award the ‘Nav Ratna’ or ‘Mini Ratna’ status
to the PSUs and whether any Major Port fulfills the eligibility condition to be declared as a ‘ratna’
port, the Committee was informed that the Navratna status is offered to PSEs, which gives a
company enhanced financial and operational autonomy and empowers it to invest up to Rs.1000
crore of 15% of their net worth on a single project without seeking Government approval. In a
year, these companies can spend up to 30% of their net worth not exceeding Rs.1000 crore. They
will also have the freedom to enter joint ventures from alliances and float subsidiaries abroad.
296. Further, Navratna status is conferred by Department of Public Enterprises. To be qualified
as a Navratna, the company must obtain a score of 60 (out of 100). The score is based on six
parameters which include net profit to net worth, total manpower cost to total cost of production
or cost of services, PBDIT to turnover, EPS (Earning Per Share) and inter-sectoral performance.
Additionally, a company must first be a Miniratna and have four independent directors on its board
before it can be made a Navratna. This classification is applicable only to PSUs and cannot be
applied to port Trust.
297. The Committee is of the view that there is an urgent need to revamp on the decision
making mechanism in the Government as regards the developmental works of the Ports so
that every project may be implemented as per the requirement of the individual Ports
separately and there should be flexibility to them for competing with the private Ports at
their close vicinity. The promptness in decision making is a very requirement for the
sustaining of the Major Ports.
298. The Committee notes that the Ministry is in the process of corporatization of the
Ports. After corporatization the Major Ports would be in a position to have more financial
powers as per the delegation of powers applicable to the PSUs.
299. The Committee is of the opinion that the Major Ports require a more refined
expertise in order to compete with their counterparts in the private sector. The Committee,
however, desires that Government should handle the matter of corporatization of Ports
carefully as many of the port employees’ unions are very much concerned about job security

52
of the employees after corporatization. They have the fear that corporatization is an initial
step for privatization. It is learnt that in the month of March, 2011, there were
demonstrations by the workers of the Visakhapatnam Port and Dock against the
corporatization of Ports. JNPT workers were also on strike expressing their solidarity with
the workers of Visakhapatnam Port. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
Government should take employees’ union into confidence and take every step to instill
confidence amongst the employees about their job security so that there is no resentment
amongst the employees against the corporatization of Ports.
300. The Committee further recommends that Government should take up the review of
administrative structure of the Major Ports with a view to ensure the improvement in
efficiencies, services and working atmosphere in the Major Ports which would lead the Ports
to more heights in the coming days.
301. It has been brought to the notice of the Committee that many of the Major Ports are
working not only as land lords but also as money lenders. For example, the total reserves and
surplus in Jawaharlal Nehru Port is Rs.3591.39 crores wherein the interest accrued on investments
during 2009-10 is Rs.159.95 crores.
302. The Committee has the view that the surplus funds which are mostly lying idle with
ports could be utilized in a more practical manner for developing infrastructure in other
Ports by way of Inter-Port lending or making a common pool of funds.
Tariff Authority for Major Por ts (TAMP)
303. As private sector was allowed entry into the Major Ports to provide services often in
competition with the Port Trust themselves, there was a demand from the private sector for an
independent regulator to set port tariffs in order to ensure that there was no unfair competition
between themselves and the Port Trust. Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP) was set up in
March, 1997 through an amendment of the Major Port Trust Act, 1963 to fix and revise port
tariffs. All powers for fixing tariffs in major port lies with TAMP, but it has no jurisdiction over
minor Ports or private Ports. TAMP is only an authority for fixing tariffs and has no other
regulatory functions or powers. All the conservancy powers in Ports and all other regulatory
function in regard to safety etc. are vested in the Port Trust themselves. Despite considerable
degree of operational powers the port trusts formed under the Major Port Trust Act lack
teeth and suffers in executing power and authority.
304. The Committee observes that TAMP has also not been specifically mandated to
improve ef ficiencies or lay down quality of services standards in port operations. However,
the Major Port Trust Act provides that while fixing tariffs the conditions under which the
service is to be rendered can be prescribed. Using this as a mechanism, TAMP is now
seeking to relate tariff to efficiencies. But each port has its own tariff schedule and scales;
the accounting procedures are also different. The Committee, therefore, feels that it would
be necessary for TAMP in the first instance to establish some common accounting
procedures amongst Ports and move towards fixing uniform principles for fixation of tariffs;
this would go a long way towards promoting inter-port competition.
305. However, the Committee is also of the view that with private investment coming in
shipping industry, in view of competition in the port sector Government should consider
setting up a tribunal to hear complaints against port tariffs.
306. The Committee is of the view that to strengthen Major Ports, a policy whereby the
two Acts, namely Indian Ports Act, 1908 and Major Ports Act, 1963, can be amalgamated

53
into a single Act should be conceived. The consolidated Act should oversee operation of both
major and minor ports in India as both the Acts have become old and outdated. Since the
inception of these two Acts, the Indian shipping sector has undergone tremendous
transformation in its working structure, with significant private participation now being
witnessed in the sector.
307. With the coming of minor ports in the country, the pace of development has
slackened for the Major Ports. Since minor ports are governed by the Indian Ports Act, 1908
and are outside the purview of the Tariff Authority of Major Ports (TAMP), a single
comprehensive Act will provide a level playing field to the Major Ports in terms of
infrastructure development, better railway networking etc. Currently, the tariff structure
also differs to a great extent for major and minor ports of the country, which needs to be
bridged.
308. To develop Indian ports to global norms there is an urgent need for the Government
to change its role from a regulator to being a facilitator. There is an urgent requirement
for aggressive second generation regulatory reforms, backed by the requisite legal and fiscal
changes to give Indian Ports a competitive edge in the global market.
309. A port promotion council could be formulated to take initiative on the developmental
activities as well as the proper marketing of the services available with the Port. Since the
performances of the Ports are little bit negative during the last years, it would be more
desirable if proper monitoring on the performance be made regularly with immediate
measures to rectify the faults and drawbacks.
Income Tax
310. The Major Ports are constituted and duly notified under the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963
and are autonomous bodies administered by statutory Board of Trustees constituted by the Central
Government. All Major Ports were allowed exemption under Section 10(20) of the Income Tax Act,
1961 as they were recognized as ‘local authority’. However, with the insertion of an explanation
of sub section 20 of Section 10 of Income Tax Act, 1961 with effect from 1.4.2002 the tax
authorities have excluded Major Ports from the ambit of prevailing benefits of exemption in
taxation.
311. It is pertinent to mention here that the Major Ports invest their revenues for maintenance
and development of infrastructure facilities which are utilized on a common user basis by trade and
industry and hence they provide essential services for the growth of trade and commerce in the
country. The investment on maintenance and development of infrastructure facilities ultimately
benefits the general public in way of supplementing to growth of trade and commerce in the
country. Exemption from income-tax would enable Ports to charge less thereby bringing down the
transaction cost for trade. There, they should be covered by sub clause (iii) of the explanation.
Department of Revenue has been accordingly, requested in December, 2009 to include sub
Clause (v) in the explanation to Section 10(20) which may read as “Board of Major Ports as
referred to under Section 3 of Major Port Trust Act, 1963”.
312. The above inclusion in the Explanation will restore the exemption status of Major Port
Trusts from taxation under Section 10(20) of the Income Tax Act which existed prior to 1.4.2002.
313. The Committee is of the view that Public Sector entities which are not purely
commercial units have to meet social obligations. To help in further welfare objective of the
Government must be viewed differently and be kept out of the purview of the income tax.
The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry of Shipping may take necessary
action to include the sub-clause (v) in the explanation to Section 10(20) of the Income Tax

54
Act in order to restore the income tax exemption to the Major Ports as requested by the
Ministry.
Public Private Partnership
314. W ith the opening up of the Indian economy, the Government has allowed private sector
participation in Major Ports to infuse funds, induct latest state-of-the-art technology, improve
management practices and above all for addition of the capacity. FDI upto 100% under automatic
route is permitted for construction and maintenance of Ports and harbour. To encourage private
sector participation, uniformity, clarity and transparency in the bidding process are important Model
Request for Qualification (RFQ) and Request for Proposal (RFP) have been finalized. A Model
Concession Agreement (MCA) has been finalized to bring uniformity in the Concession Agreements.
TAMP fix the charges to be paid by the port users by the private operators.
315. The Committee was informed that it is the policy decision of the Government of India and
direction of Planning Commission to go for PPP mode for the commercially viable projects to
attract private investment, latest technology and advantage of efficient management available with
private sector. Already there is a huge gap between infrastructure development and requirement of
funds through budgetary supports. The Major Ports are not restricted to replace the cargo handling
equipments and mechanization of the berths and terminals that are being run by the Ports. There
is no direction from the Government of India to outsource the profitable activities. The Ports Trust
Boards are free to take a commercial decision on the new projects based on the level of investment
required vis-à-vis the spare investible funds and timelines of the projects subject to Government
approvals.
316. The Committee was informed that the PPP project are chosen among all the Major Ports
depending upon their commercial viability where private investment is expected to be forthcoming.
Almost all the Major Ports have awarded them. As per the policy of the Government private sector
investments should be invited in the commercially viable projects to increase the capacity of the
Ports vis-à-vis the anticipated traffic. The Ports are to invest their internal funds to finance the
projects that provide common user facilities like faster evacuation, construction of break-water,
maintenance dredging, capital dredging etc. which enhances the competitiveness of the Ports. The
PPP Projects are awarded on the basis of standard and transparent bidding documents with two
stage bidding. The projects are implemented through a Model Concession Agreement (MCA) after
rigorous appraisal and approval process which provides for sharing of risk among the Government/
Project Authority vis-à-vis the investors and private players.
317. The Committee observed that Joint Venture projects get delayed because of lack of
proper guidelines and standard documents. The Committee recommends that the
Government may make proper guidelines in this regard for a speedy disposal of such
projects.
318. The Committee also notes that Concession Agreements have not been kept at pace
with the development and the growth of containerization in India. The Committee
recommends that the Concession Agreements should be reformulated keeping in mind the
national interest and to avoid any monopoly or unilateral actions by the private participants.
319. In  the current year 2010-11, 6 PPP projects have been awarded at an estimated cost of
Rs.2693.08 crores and capacity of 33 MT. These include a Container Terminal at Ennore Port Ltd.,

Kandla Port. 29 private sector projects, are already operational and 20 projects are under

321. The Committee notes that the private partners eventually use the operating right as
captive facility. They levy certain extraneous charges and claim that such charges do not
form part of revenue eligible to be shared with the Port Trust.
322. Under the name of privatization, foreign shipping cartels are getting a foot hold in
the centre of economic activities of our country. It has been propagated that privatization
will introduce competition and will reduce the Port charges but in reality, Multinational
Companies are charging more terminal handling charges than the Major Ports.
323. Profit making services are taken over by the multinational companies leaving
behind unremunerated services with the Port Trust which may convert the Ports as loss
making units. This has taken away the job of thousands of workers working in the
Ports.
324. The Committee recommends that Government should examine the experience and
performance of PPP abroad particularly in countries which have been the mother of the PPP
contracts. It would not be in the interest of the nation to allow foreign MNCs to take over
the port related activities. Moreover, the Ports have strategic Naval defence systems within

Major and Minor Ports
325. The Committee was informed that Indian Ports have generally been facing the problem of
congestion due to spurt in the cargo after liberalization as the capacity of the Ports lagged behind
vis-à-vis the traffic growth as per the normal accepted parameters of 70% utilization of the berths
and terminals. There is no significant impact on the growth of the Major Ports by operationalisation

330. The Committee was informed that in the container segment’ which is one of the growing
sectors in the EXIM-trade, almost all the Major Ports witnessed growth despite establishing large
number of private ports and private operators. The total number of vessels at the Major Ports also

331. In Orissa POSCO port near Paradip was sanctioned although it was felt that a new port
